International Business Management: Study Map

Lectures 1-4 (7, 14, 21 and 28 October 2026), Prof. Abdel Salam Abu Qahf, EMBA MIDOR 1. Built for Ahmed Sabri from the class transcripts, the three handouts, classmates' and Ahmed's own notes, the review booklet, past exams and the online search.

Online copy of this page: ahmedsabri.me/ib-study-map (GitHub repository Amsamms/ib-study-map). This file itself works offline, with everything inside it.

The mind map is organized by logic, in the order a company meets each idea when it goes abroad, with links that explain how the ideas connect. "Follow the story" walks you through it step by step.

How to use this page
  • Story (top bar, or the button above): the whole course, lectures 1-4 with the handouts and the cases, as one short continuous story (about 1,900 words) to see what it is all about before studying the details. It remembers where you stopped.
  • Mind map (top bar, or the button above): the whole course as one connected tree, organized by logic rather than by branch number. Tap a box to read it and see what it links to; Follow the story walks through the ideas in order and says how each one leads to the next.
  • Read top-down. Each numbered branch starts with a short story, then sub-branches you open one by one. Tick the box on a sub-branch when you have understood it; the thin bar at the top shows your progress (saved in this browser only).
  • Layers. The bold core points are always visible. Below them, closed boxes: Explain it simply, What he said in class (his exact words), Original handout text, His views, plus classmates' photos. Open them when you want more; ignore them when you don't.
  • Core only (top bar) hides every extra layer, booklet box, photo and source tag: the page becomes a short revision sheet.
  • Coloured boxes: Booklet extra points from the earlier-batch review booklet; Class vs handout where sources disagree, with advice; Memory aid my mnemonics; Modern example my examples, not his.
  • Grey tags show where each point comes from (see the Sources branch).
  • Who is who. "He", "his", "the lecturer" always means our professor, Prof. Abdel Salam Abu Qahf. Names in the grey tags are classmates who shared material: GOMAA (audio transcripts of lectures 1-2), Eng. Mohamed Abdelaal (lecture 3 transcript, compiled notes, Quiz 1), Dr. Mahmoud Elsere (handwritten lecture 3 notes), Ahmed Awad (handwritten lecture 1 notes), Ahmed Amir (summary of the Myth reading), Masr and SEIF (posted the review booklet and past exams). Any other name (Vernon, Levitt, Watson ...) is a scholar or author, introduced where it first appears.
  • Exam words. Papers A to K = 11 of his past exam papers from earlier batches, lettered by me (all listed in the Exam corner). The DBA exam = a final exam on the same subject from Alexandria University's EDBA (Executive Doctorate in Business Administration) program, shared by Dr. Elsere. The booklet = a 45-page Arabic review booklet from earlier batches. The handouts = the two readings he gave out: "The Myth of Globalization" (lecture 2) and Chapter 7 on political risk and negotiations (lecture 3).
  • Test yourself at the end of each branch: think of the answer, then tap to check.
  • Print prints the map with explanations; Print all also prints quotes and originals (long).
  • Everything about the exam (priorities, past questions, model answers) is in the Exam corner, away from the study map.

Story

Karim had just finished his EMBA when his father, who owned a small juice company in Alexandria called Nile Juice, asked him whether they should start selling outside Egypt. Karim realized he was being asked to enter international business, and he wanted to understand what that really meant.

He found that it was nothing new. The merchants of Quraysh travelled to Syria in summer and to Yemen in winter, buying in one land and selling in another, and the Phoenicians and Greeks had traded abroad long before them. Only the name was new. He learned that international business is the application of all managerial functions, theories and principles in different environments: a manager abroad plans, organizes, motivates and decides exactly as at home, and only the environment around him changes. In practice, any organization doing business in one or more foreign countries, directly or indirectly, is an international business. He also came across an old definition by a scholar named Vernon, by which a firm is international only if it works in six or more countries with sales of 100 million dollars a year, and he saw why it was wrong: the line was drawn at a random place, and one foreign country is enough.

His father asked why, if the job is the same, so many companies fail abroad. Karim told him about an HR manager at MIDOR whose money-based bonus plan worked well in Egypt but failed when she copied it in the UAE, where people already earn more and a little extra money does not move them. He told him how Gaddafi forced 7-Up, Mirinda and Coca-Cola to take Arabic names in Libya, how Pepsi painted its cans blue for the Philippines, how McDonald's dropped beef in India, and how Cadbury replaced pig fat with vegetable oil in Egypt. He explained that Western and Egyptian companies give each worker one boss, while Japanese companies decide nothing until everyone agrees, and that this consensus style, invented in America, succeeded only in Japan, because Japanese culture puts the group first while American and Arab cultures put the individual first. The principles of management are the same everywhere, but culture, economy, politics and society change how they work.

So Karim learned not to trust only the facts in front of him. Like the puzzle of joining nine dots with three lines, the answer often lies outside the picture you are given. He remembered a case from his EMBA about an American company choosing between Jane and Bill to run marketing for its Saudi subsidiary. The answer depended on questions the case did not answer: cosmetics would favour Jane and steel or cars would favour Bill, and conservative Riyadh would favour Bill while Jeddah would favour Jane. A good manager asks, assumes and imagines scenarios, and does not judge people by stereotypes.

Before going anywhere, Karim had to ask whether the core of his product could travel. A product is anything, tangible or intangible, that satisfies a human need, and it has three layers: the core benefit people buy it for, the formal features such as size and colour, and the augmented services such as a guarantee. The core must stay the same abroad, while the features and services can adapt. He also learned that a market is not a place but a group of people with a need, a desire to buy and the money to pay. People in Sudan and Saudi Arabia wanted a cheap, tasty, healthy drink and could pay for it, so the core of his juice could travel.

There were two ways to go. He could go indirectly, by exporting juice made in Alexandria, or directly, by building his own plant abroad, either fully owned or as a joint venture with a local partner, who could even pay for the plant while Nile Juice brought its know-how. Karim started by exporting to Sudan.

Years later Nile Juice had companies in several countries, and people started calling it a multinational, which means a cluster of companies in different countries controlled by one headquarters. Karim learned the difference between a multidomestic company, where each country unit runs its own way, and a global company, which makes its products and policies the same worldwide, like Coca-Cola and McDonald's. The United Nations prefers the word transnational, because in poor countries that were once colonies the word foreign sounds like colonization. A global company looks for similarities between countries, such as one Arabic advert for all Arab countries, because making one product for many markets lowers the cost of each unit. Companies also differ in who decides: in an ethnocentric company headquarters decides everything, in a polycentric one each country decides for itself, in a regiocentric one each region decides, and a geocentric company is a large company integrated vertically, owning more steps of its chain from farm to shop, or horizontally, repeating the same operation in many places.

A consultant told Karim to make everything the same everywhere, because the world had become a small village. Karim checked. Globalization means the free movement of everything between countries without any restriction, yet people still need visas, products must meet the standards of each bloc, like the CE mark in Europe, and conflicts between countries are everywhere. Faster flights and cheap calls had brought the death of distance, not globalization. Trade agreements like GATT and GATS push toward it, and burgers and jeans everywhere only look like it. Agreements between rich and poor countries give equal opportunities but never equal results, as Egyptian exporters learned when their potatoes were rejected by European standards, or when a shipment of fine Egyptian cotton undershirts was refused in England because the pins rusted at sea. Globalization, Karim concluded, is a myth.

That did not mean a different juice for every country. A global product can be sold worldwide with small local touches, and a company can think global and act local. Karim read an old debate on this. In 1983 Theodore Levitt claimed that needs were becoming the same everywhere, that people would accept a standard product for a lower price, and that one product for the world would bring huge savings. In 1987 Douglas and Wind replied in "The Myth of Globalization" that people are not becoming the same, that cheap prices are easy to attack, and that modern factories can make many versions cheaply. Standardizing works only when there is a group of similar buyers across countries, real gains from sharing, and worldwide channels to reach them, and it is blocked by government rules, different shops and media, different materials and competitors, existing partners and resisting local managers. The choice is a scale, not yes or no, and most companies sit in the middle. Karim kept one juice and one brand but adapted bottle sizes, prices and adverts.

He then mapped what surrounds his company. Every organization lives inside its own internal environment, a task environment of its customers, suppliers, competitors and government agencies, and a general environment of economy, politics, culture, society and technology. He saw politics at work in Egypt between 2011 and 2013, when instability drove foreign firms out and kept new ones away. He also remembered buying a can of Pepsi without a question and then questioning a Kia salesman about everything: the same man was two different customers, because one purchase was emotional and the other rational. When he studied a rival in Saudi Arabia, he did not just summarize it; he built a fact sheet comparing both companies on their origin, business, customers, diversification, entry methods, strengths and weaknesses, the way Illy and Starbucks can be compared, and only then drew his conclusions.

When Nile Juice built a plant abroad, the government soon capped its prices and limited the profits it could send home. Karim was facing political risk, the likelihood that the host country's political decisions or events will hurt a foreign firm's investment, operations or profit transfers. Unlike uncertainty, a risk can be predicted and calculated, which is why insurers cover risks. It can hit every firm in the country, through violence, corruption or constant political change, or target only certain firms, through a special tax or the seizure of a plant. Governments can block imports, fix prices, impose quotas, block profits and salaries, expropriate a company with compensation, or confiscate and nationalize it without compensation. Karim learned to watch for warning signs: unemployment and inflation, frequent changes of government, deep cultural divisions, and hostility between his home country and the host. To protect himself he could integrate into the country, with local partners, suppliers, workers and research, or defend himself by keeping a small footprint, borrowing from local banks and spreading production across countries. He chose a mix, and he learned that keeping something the host cannot do without, such as technology, keeps the government's hands off. When the terms had to be agreed, he negotiated patiently, knowing that culture shapes every step of a deal.

Competition was the other danger. Companies like Coca-Cola have lived for more than a century because they can compete any time, anywhere, any way and against anybody, built on total quality management, continuous learning and world-class standards. Quality needs a vision shared by every worker, a variety of products, empowered employees and constant comparison with the best, and money spent on quality saves more than it costs, as Xerox learned when Japanese copiers forced it to improve. Karim also read Richard Watson's forecast that by 2027 only 25 of 500 large American companies and 24 of 100 British ones would survive. The dying ones show clear signs: skilled people leaving, cuts in marketing, no new customers for six months, poor service, no new products for a year, rejected ideas, piling stock, an aging board, dependence on one supplier, flattery instead of truth, weak information and fighting owners. When Karim found that 94 percent of his bottles came from a single supplier, he found a second one the same week.

Surviving was only the start. The companies that last adapt all the time, and they learn by improving in small steps rather than waiting for one big leap. That needs people who are free to create and who believe they can make a difference, and an open eye on everything that goes in and comes out: if the results are poor, change the inputs or the process. A company with quality and learning joins the club of the world's best, which puts the customer first, manages its people creatively, uses modern technology, treats its suppliers as partners and keeps justice at work. Getting in is easy and staying is hard, so Karim kept up his research, built good information, sold covers and cups beside the juice, stayed close to his customers because none of them is loyal and a new one costs twice an old one, moved fast, kept things simple, made one promise and kept it, and smiled. When he planned a factory abroad he scored each candidate country out of 100, weighting the economy above politics, and chose the highest. For each new market he also asked how much of his marketing could stay the same: it depended on the product, how alike the buyers were, which media reached them and in what language, the government's rules, the roads and services, and the relations between the two countries.

Nile Juice now sells in four countries, and before every decision Karim still asks himself what he does not know yet.

Lectures in brief

Lecture 1: Introduction to international business

7 Oct 2026. Sources: Gomaa's transcript, Awad's notes, Abdelaal's compiled notes.

1. How to solve a case full branch

  • The case text is never enough: make assumptions, ask questions, build more than one scenario.
  • Bill or Jane (US firm's Saudi subsidiary needs a marketing manager; Jane 10 years + EMBA, Bill 8 years): the industry decides (cosmetics = Jane; steel, electronics, car assembly = Bill) and the city decides (Riyadh, conservative = Bill; Jeddah or Abha = Jane). "Neutrality is always required"; avoid stereotyping.
  • Creativity puzzles: 9 dots with 3 lines (go outside the box); how many cubes (6, not 1); rectangles in a square; the handkerchief's highest point is its centre (الوسطية = the top, not a weak middle).

2. Definition 1 of international business full branch

  • The same management functions (plan, organize, direct, decide, control) and theories, in different environments.
  • MIDOR example: a money-based incentive plan worked at MIDOR but failed in the UAE / Aramco, because a higher living standard makes money motivate less.

3. Adapting to local culture

  • Libya (Gaddafi): 7Up became Al-Sab'a, Mirinda became Mrada, Coca-Cola became Al-Shafi.
  • Philippines: Pepsi cans mostly blue. India: McDonald's dropped beef (chicken, fish, soy). Egypt: Cadbury replaced pig fat with vegetable oil.
  • Watch verbal habits and body language too.

4. Management across cultures

  • Unity of command (USA, 1916): orders from one manager only. Based on individualism (US, West, Egypt, Arab world).
  • Management by consensus (Japan): no decision without 100% yes; "success is the responsibility of all, failure is the responsibility of all". Based on collectivism and Kaizen. The Americans tried to copy it and failed.

5. What is international business? full branch

  • Old practice, new name: Phoenicians, Greek merchants, the winter and summer journeys (Surah Quraysh) = the first indirect IB.
  • Definition 2 (professional): any organization doing business in one or more foreign markets, directly or indirectly. No minimum; no definition is accepted worldwide.
  • Indirect = exporting (Farag Allah becomes international once it sells in Sudan). Direct = own plant or subsidiary abroad, wholly owned or a joint venture (the local partner can pay, the foreign one brings only know-how). His own "Egyptian model" of entry modes comes later. full branch
  • Vernon: 6+ foreign markets AND $100M annual turnover. He calls it "completely wrong" (what about $99M?). full branch

6. Terms for international firms full branch

  • Multinational: a cluster of companies in several countries controlled by HQ.
  • Multidomestic: each affiliate sets its own strategies, based on local differences.
  • Global: very large; standardizes and integrates operations, products, marketing, HR worldwide (Coca-Cola, Pepsi, McDonald's), only minor changes.
  • Transnational: the UN's term, avoiding the colonial image of "multinational" or "foreign".

7. Product and market full branch

  • Product: anything tangible or intangible (services, ideas, persons, impressions) that satisfies a need. Three levels: core (the "why", function or benefit), formal (size, colour, weight, features), augmented (guarantee, free cover, instalments).
  • Rule: if the core can be internationalized, go; if not, stay home. Formal and augmented levels take minor local changes.
  • Market: people with a need, a desire to buy and purchasing power. "The market is not a place." full branch

8. Globalization is "a big myth" full branch

  • Two definitions: free mobility of everything between countries without restrictions; a tendency toward integrating the world.
  • Myth: visas, restrictions, disputes (USA-Iran, Egypt-Ethiopia, Algeria-Morocco); the EU is a regional agreement, not globalization.
  • Hamburgers, jeans, Coca-Cola = superficial symptoms.
  • Driving forces (not globalization itself): GATT (goods), GATS (services), transport and communication technology; political, economic, technological forces. "As long as there are restrictions, don't talk about globalization." full branch

9. Global management full branch

  • The management team's 3 objectives: (1) search worldwide for opportunities; (2) keep a presence in key markets; (3) exploit similarities among countries (one Arabic advert for 22 countries) = economies of scale.
  • Classifying MNCs (other bases: technological, political, technical, nationality): ethnocentric (centralized, HQ decides all), polycentric (decentralized, each subsidiary sets its policies), geocentric (large, integrated), regiocentric (regional). full branch
  • Vertical integration: upward toward the market (own stores) or downward toward raw materials (cotton farms). Horizontal: the same operation in several places (Alexandria, Tanta, Damanhur, Marsa Matruh).

Homework: Starbucks report; Bill or Jane questions.

Lecture 2: Case method, environment, globalization, standardization

14 Oct 2026. Sources: Gomaa's transcript, Abdelaal's compiled notes, the Myth of Globalization reading.

1. Mission vs strategy full branch

  • Mission: what the company aims to be and why it exists. Strategy: the paths it chooses to reach its objectives.

2. How to answer a case (feedback on the Starbucks hand-ins) full branch

  • Most reports summarized the case, then barely touched the questions: "too general".
  • Method: (1) short briefing on each company; (2) a fact sheet comparing them factor by factor; (3) then answer, drawing suggestions, actions and lessons from the fact sheet.
  • Fact sheet factors (open list): country of origin, nature of business, degree of diversification, type of customers (B2B/B2C), degree of international commitment, entry modes, competitors, SWOT, potential, competitive advantages. "More comprehensive than the bloody SWOT"; SWOT and PESTLE sit inside it.
  • Starbucks vs Illy: "USA is a brand" (origin = strength); Starbucks diversifies into related niches (food, mugs, gifts, the in-store experience), Illy has a single product; Illy is mainly B2B, so serve end consumers too; Starbucks' weakness is very high prices.

3. The total business environment full branch

  • Internal + external general (economic, political, cultural, social, technological, international) + external task (customers, suppliers, competitors, government agencies).
  • Instability example: Egypt 2011-2013, foreign firms left and investors moved money abroad.

4. Pepsi vs Kia: same person, two customers full branch

  • Pepsi: emotional motives; buys fast, no questions, accepts an overcharge.
  • Kia: rational / economic motives: price, cash or instalments, durability, spare parts, guarantee, fuel. "All of these questions mean money."
  • So the task environments differ: competitors (Pepsi vs Coca-Cola; Kia vs carmakers and even tuk-tuks, trains, planes), suppliers, and government agencies (food vs engineering).

5. Globalization: concept vs myth full branch

  • Two definitions: integrating the world economically, politically, culturally and socially; free mobility of everything (even poverty and problems).
  • Don't confuse the concept with its driving forces (GATT, GATS, the IT and transport revolution). McDonald's, Pizza Hut, Starbucks, jeans = superficial symptoms.
  • Myth: visas (the US refusing Mahmoud Abbas), EU standards (CE mark), trade blocs. What exists is the "death of distance"; geographic and cultural distance remain; never one small village.
  • Agreements give "equal opportunities, never equal results" (Egyptian potatoes rejected on EU standards). Signing GATT/GATS without asking for help to upgrade production = "the big crime"; the blame is on the government that signed. full branch
  • Gil undershirts: Egyptian undershirts sold out in an English mall; the next order was rejected because the pins rusted at sea.

6. The global product and the 3 options full branch

  • Global product: marketable worldwide (Coca-Cola, razor blades, pens). Same test: if the core can be globalized, go.
  • Think local / act local = domestic firm. Think global / act local = minor changes (7Up written in Arabic). Think global / act global = fully standardized strategy.

7. Global standardization (the Myth of Globalization reading) full branch

  • 3 assumptions: (1) customer needs are becoming homogeneous worldwide; (2) people give up preferences (function, design) for lower price with high quality; (3) substantial economies of scale.
  • Requisite conditions (sources clash): in class he said (1) standardized product, (2) standardized marketing program, (3) a global brand. The article and Abdelaal: (1) a global market segment exists, (2) synergies from standardization, (3) international communication and distribution infrastructure. For the DBA question use the article's version. full branch
  • Constraints: internal (the firm's current operations, local managers' lack of enthusiasm); external (government trade rules, weak infrastructure, competition). full branch
  • Continuum ("continuum means scale"): Option 1 = standardization (global strategy); Option 2 = clusters of countries (same product within a cluster, different prices, one advertising strategy per cluster); Option 3 = differentiation (multidomestic, everything adapted per country). full branch

Lecture 3: Political risk, competitiveness, why companies die, TQM

21 Oct 2026. Sources: Abdelaal's transcript and compiled notes, Elsere's notes (the transcript has a gap, the notes fill it).

1. Risk vs uncertainty full branch

  • Risk: predictable, its probability can be calculated (so insurers insure it). Uncertainty: cannot be predicted or calculated.

2. Political system and political risk full branch

  • Political system: the structure, processes and activities by which a nation governs itself (Lebanon: parliament picks the president). Study it before entering.
  • Political risk: (1) a predictable, calculable event that may hurt the firm's performance or existence in the host country; (2) the likelihood that host-government policies or political practices constrain, block or paralyse the firm's investment and operations.

3. Forms of political risk full branch

  • Customs restrictions on imports or exports; price setting / ceilings; production quotas (Egypt's spinning and weaving, 1960s-70s).
  • Expropriation = taken WITH compensation; confiscation (مصادرة) and nationalization (تأميم) = WITHOUT (his class definitions).
  • Profit blockage (a French firm in Egypt not allowed to send profits home); salary limits (Libya under Gaddafi: expatriates could send home at most half their salary).

4. Macro vs micro political risk full branch

  • Macro hits all firms, domestic and foreign: all government intervention, violence (Paris, Egypt 2011), corruption, trade wars, terrorism, polarization, kidnapping, continuous political change (Egypt 2011-2015: no new FDI, foreign firms left, investors such as Sawiris moved money out).
  • Micro hits a specific firm or industry (targeted taxes, trade restrictions). From the notes and handout; the transcript does not record his definition.

5. The 4 criteria (indicators) for predicting political risk full branch

  • Economic: unemployment, falling living standards (breed corruption and crime), inflation, currency swings.
  • Political: frequent cabinet changes (6 in Egypt 2011-2013), political kidnappings, extreme party fragmentation (Lebanon).
  • Cultural: deep divisions of language, religion or region with no unifying national culture.
  • International: hostility between home and host country (Reagan barring US firms from the USSR; unstable neighbours such as Sudan and Libya).

6. Managing political risk ("V.I.P., 2 strategies") full branch

  • Integrative ("marry the country"): (1) ties with local leaders and parties; (2) maximize local manufacturing, suppliers and labour; (3) subcontract locally and form joint ventures; (4) local R&D.
  • Defensive ("keep one foot outside"): (1) small local plant; (2) locals out of key posts; (3) borrow from host-country banks (governments hesitate to nationalize firms indebted to their own banks); (4) spread operations across countries.

7. Global competitiveness full branch

  • Compete any time, anywhere, against anybody, in any way (Coca-Cola, Pepsi, Caterpillar, P&G, KFC, McDonald's).
  • 3 pillar strategies: (1) TQM; (2) the learning organization; (3) the World Class Organization.

8. Why companies die (Richard Watson) full branch

  • Study of 600 firms in 2017 (500 US, 100 UK): by 2027 only 25 US and 24 UK firms survive; the rest fail to keep modernizing the pillars.
  • Red flags (Elsere 12; Abdelaal 10, without no. 11 and with no. 9 as a separate ratio): (1) skilled staff resign (bad pay, injustice, no promotion, bad leadership, poor conditions); (2) under-investment in marketing; (3) no new customers in 6 months; (4) poor after-sales; (5) no new product or size/colour variant in 12 months; (6) refusing new ideas (Kodak, Nokia); (7) excess inventory, low turnover; (8) no strategic planning, aging board; (9) dependence on one supplier, customer or manpower source; (10) hypocrisy and flattery ("Lie is very dangerous"); (11) inefficient information systems; (12) owners and partners fighting.
  • Marketing myopia sits at flag 7 in Elsere's notes, at flag 6 in Abdelaal's.
  • External flexibility (dependency) ratio = one supplier's purchases / total purchases x 100; higher ratio = less flexibility (the supplier controls you). The worked example differs: 90.9% (Abdelaal) vs 94.3% (Elsere). full branch

9. TQM full branch

  • 4 requirements (Elsere; Abdelaal has 3, without the first): (1) quality vision ("the company's life and your job security depend on quality"); (2) product diversification; (3) empowerment (freedom in the job, no micromanagement, accountability for results, full information and authority); (4) benchmarking (learn from a role model: father, teacher, industry leader).
  • Objective vs target: objective = long term (continuity); target = short term (immediate profit).
  • Quality-cost graph: vertical = cost of quality control, horizontal = defective units, falling curve (7,000 gives 50 defects; 9,000 gives 30). Managers: quality spending saves cost in the end and keeps customers. Engineers: it is extra upfront cost. full branch
  • Xerox: Japanese firms replaced metal parts with plastic, cutting cost while keeping quality. full branch

Homework: the "Going to Gdansk" case (p. 208).

Lecture 4: FDI split, sustaining world class, standardization factors

28 Oct 2026. Source: Ahmed's handwritten notes (14 pages; no transcript yet). Reading: the Ch3 handout "Global Competitiveness" (branch 9).

1. Salient determinants (FDI) full branch

  • 80% of world FDI goes to developed nations; the remaining 20% = 16% China + 4% other nations. All countries have FDI.

2. Global competitiveness again: adaptation full branch

  • Coca-Cola and similar firms succeeded with the 4 any's because they adapt: "adaptation is the success of each story", "a winning word".
  • Fortune magazine (and the Economist) select the top 500 in each category worldwide.
  • They adopted 3 major strategies: TQM, learning organization, WCO.

3. TQM prerequisites (the 4 again) full branch

  • (1) Vision (what quality means to the company); (2) diversity; (3) empowerment; (4) benchmark.

4. Learning organization full branch

  • = adaptation + continuous improvement. Improvement = small changes; development = huge changes (improvement, not development).
  • 3 requirements (a triangle): creativity / innovation, openness, self-efficacy.
  • Self-efficacy is tied to empowerment: encourage people to think and create.
  • Openness: inputs (political, economic, cultural variables + laws + labour + machines) → operation → outputs; output not satisfactory = reconsider inputs or operation. "Openness is information" (companies die from missing or poor information).
  • Creativity = something new with no previous example; the ideation part of innovation. Innovation = applied creativity, "not canned ideas". Giza pyramid: new, no precedent, passes the time test.

5. World Class Organization ("the club") full branch

  • TQM + learning organization qualify a company to join.
  • Class gave 5: (1) customer oriented; (2) creative HRM (incentives, promotion, gathering talents, healthy conditions, salaries); (3) advanced technology; (4) look after suppliers (they save time and inventory cost and advise you; the pharmacy pays after it sells); (5) justice in the working climate ("no production with injustice"). The handout and booklet have 6: add continuous improvement.
  • "Easy to become world class, not easy to sustain it."

6. The Gdansk (Poland) fact sheet full branch

  • A weighted table: factors (political stability 20, economic environment 60 with market size, ...; total 100), Poland's score per factor (15 of the 20 for politics), total calculated.
  • Add a column per market (Poland, Egypt): the highest total wins.

7. How to sustain and develop world class (18 ways) full branch

  • (1) Continuous R&D (new products; better or cheaper existing ones; new technology; better production methods; efficiency); (2) a good database (quality, quantity, timing of information); (3) an add-on product ("mobile cover"); (4) customer intimacy (expectations, participation, his shoes, his needs); (5) continuous value added (best use on the pack, follow-up, advice) = customer retention; a new customer costs double; (6) new techniques for the market.
  • (7) Strategic alliances and JVs (supplier, retailer, wholesaler); (8) global partnership with global firms; (9) a global team; (10) capitalize on the waves of generations (Uncle El-Sayed sold the grandfather tobacco and gave the boy a bonbon: the next generation loved him too); (11) simplicity "always wins"; (12) 6 selling appeals with 5 kept are worse than 1 kept.
  • (13) Invest in marketing; (14) speed (response, market entry, everything); (15) diversify the weapons against competitors (more cards, more potential); (16) grasp competitors' success factors; (17) continuous audit of everything; (18) smile.
  • "Customer loyalty" is old school: no loyal customers, each follows his own interest; now it is customer retention. Understand the customer better than competitors.

8. Factors that govern the degree of standardization full branch

  • A global firm should standardize its procedures (marketing mix; plan, product, distribution, policy), but 6 factors decide how far: (1) type of product (the core layer; "convenience products"); (2) heterogeneity / homogeneity of markets; (3) media characteristics (TV coverage, language, culture: a Thai car advert is out of Egyptian ethics); (4) government restrictions (price ceiling, quota, import and export limits, to protect national firms); (5) availability of infrastructure services (or build your own); (6) type of political relationship.

Next assignment: "What is a global manager?"

1What is international business?

Start with a camel caravan. Long before anyone wrote a textbook, the merchants of Quraysh took goods north to Syria in summer and south to Yemen in winter, buying in one country and selling in another. That is international business. The name is new; the practice is very old.

In this branch you meet the two definitions that our lecturer, Prof. Abdel Salam Abu Qahf ("he" on this page), gave in lecture 1, and the two ways a firm can cross a border: indirectly (send your goods) or directly (set up your own operation there). You will also meet a definition he rejects. A scholar named Vernon (he only called him "a well-known scholar") said a firm counts as international only if it operates in 6 or more foreign countries and has sales of $100 million a year. Prof. Abu Qahf calls this "completely wrong": why should a firm in 5 countries, or with $99 million, not count?

An old practice with a new name
  • The term "international business" (as a school or a science) is new; the practice has "a long, long history". L1 transcript, part 2
  • The Phoenicians and Greek merchants sent representatives abroad to buy and sell. L1 transcript
  • Surah Quraysh, رحلة الشتاء والصيف (the winter and summer journeys, Hijaz to Syria and Yemen): he calls it the first indirect form of international business (export and import). L1 transcript; Awad notes
What he said in class
"International business as a terminology is new ... But in practice, it has a long, long, long history ... since the Phoenician civilization."
"The winter trip and the summer trip represent the first form of indirect international business ... Trade. Export and import. From Hijaz to Syria and Lebanon and Jordan ... And to Yemen as well."
L1 transcript, part 2
Two definitions of international business

He gave two definitions. Learn both, word for word: he insists on exact words.

Definition 1: the managerial one
"[International business] is the application of all managerial functions and theories and principles in different environments."
Plain meaning: an international manager does the same job as a local one (plan, organize, direct, lead, decide, control, using the same principles and theories), but in different environments. The difference is the environment, not the job.
"different environments" is the key phrase. Without it, the definition just describes ordinary management.
L1 transcript, parts 1 and 2
Definition 2: the professional (practical) one
"International business represents any organization that is doing business in one or more than one foreign market, or foreign country ... either in a direct way or indirect way."
Plain meaning: one foreign market is enough. There is no cut-off point: "no 'at least' or 'at most'".
His definition counts the number of foreign markets as "one or more". Vernon's counts six or more (see below).
L1 transcript, part 2
  • "There is no common definition for international business", no single definition accepted worldwide. All are acceptable except extreme ones like Vernon's. L1 transcript
Explain it simply

Think of yourself at MIDOR. If you moved to a refinery in the UAE you would still plan, organize, motivate and control. What changes is everything around you: the culture, the laws, the economy, what motivates people. Definition 1 says exactly that. Definition 2 is the test you use to decide whether a company is international: has it done business in at least one country outside its home? Then yes.

The textbook gives a third, shorter version: international business is "any commercial transaction that crosses the borders of two or more nations". Textbook (Wild and Wild) p. 28

What he said in class
"In other words, the international manager is practicing the same functions of the local one. But, and a big but: in different environments! In different environments!"
"You are going to follow the same steps of making a decision ... specify the problem ... develop alternatives ... evaluate alternatives ... select an alternative, and ... issue your decision. The same steps, but in different situations."
"There's no cut-off point in the number of countries to be served by the firm concerned ... there is no 'at least' or 'at most'."
L1 transcript
Two ways to cross the border: indirect and direct

A company that wants to go international has two major options: L1 transcript

Indirect غير مباشرDirect مباشر
WhatSell abroad without building your own operation there. His example: exporting.Build your own factory, plant, subsidiary, affiliate or branch in the foreign market (direct foreign investment).
His exampleFaragalla (the Egyptian juice and food company) becomes an international firm once its product is sold in Sudan, Libya, Kuwait or Lebanon.Faragalla builds its own plant in Saudi Arabia, Libya or Sudan. "Just one country" is enough.
Ownership(no ownership abroad)Wholly owned, or a joint venture (JV) with a local partner.
  • In a JV the foreign firm can join without investing money: the local partner pays the cost and the foreign firm contributes know-how. L1 transcript
  • More indirect forms ("more than four") and direct forms come later under modes of entry into foreign markets, including an entry model of his own that he called the "Egyptian model" (not explained yet). L1 transcript (see the Coming later branch)
Memory aid Indirect = my goods travel. Direct = my company travels.
What he said in class
"Once the company succeeded in exporting its product to a certain ... foreign market, it becomes an international firm."
"The company can enter a JV, or joint venture basis, without investing money. The cost of investment project ... is actually paid by the local partner, while the foreign firm is participating, let's say, by know-how."
L1 transcript, part 2
Vernon's definition, and why he calls it wrong
Vernon's definition of an international firm
A firm is international if it invests in six or more foreign markets and makes an annual turnover of 100 million dollars a year.
Two conditions, both required. Well known, but he says "completely wrong" because the cut-off is arbitrary: what about a firm that makes 99 million dollars?
Ahmed Awad's notes wrote "$100M investment"; the transcript says "annual turnover". Use "annual turnover", as in the transcript.
L1 transcript; Awad notes
His views

"Vernon ... has defined the international firm in a very funny way ... completely wrong, from my own viewpoint." He said he debated his professor at Strathclyde University, Prof. James Dennison, on this "and I won the debate". L1 transcript

Booklet p. 2: other definitions

Foreign company: owns, manages or indirectly practises an investment activity (production, marketing or services) outside the home country, regardless of the number of host countries.

Livingstone (like the other names in this box, a scholar the booklet cites): the international company has an independent legal personality (not controlled by any home government) and chooses to invest in one or more foreign countries. Vernon focused on size; Livingstone on freedom (choice).

Hood and Young: owns and manages investment projects in more than one foreign country. Rolfe: international when foreign sales, foreign employees or foreign investment reach about 25% of the total.

Booklet p. 3 question: are airline, tourism and commercial-agency offices abroad international companies? No (Livingstone): the nature of their business forces them to have offices (no element of choice), and a commission agent or distributor abroad is not an international company.

Same management, different environments: stories to remember

His main lesson of lecture 1: the functions and principles of management are the same everywhere, but divergences between countries (culture, economy, politics, society) change how you plan, decide and motivate. A manager must recognize these differences. L1 transcript

Story 1: the MIDOR incentive plan that failed in the UAE

An HR manager at MIDOR designs a money-based incentive scheme that works very well. She moves to a company in the UAE and copies it. It fails. Why? The standard of living there is higher, so extra money motivates people less ("take it for yourself"). In Egypt, with a lower standard of living, money motivates well. L1 transcript

Story 2: brands that changed their names or looks

  • Libya: Gaddafi required name changes: 7-Up became السبعة "Al-Sab'a" (the seven), Mirinda became "Mrada" (a village between Benghazi and Ras Lanuf), Coca-Cola became الشافي "Al-Shafi" (the healer). He visited Mrada in 1991 or 1992. L1 transcript
  • Philippines: Pepsi was asked to make its cans mostly blue; Filipinos preferred blue. L1 transcript
  • India: cows are sacred, so McDonald's replaced beef with chicken, fish and soy burgers rather than give up a huge market. L1 transcript
  • Egypt: Cadbury replaced animal (pig) fat with vegetable oil. L1 transcript
  • Also watch verbal habits and body language (hands, eyes, facial expressions). L1 transcript

Story 3: unity of command vs management by consensus

Unity of commandوحدة الأمر
Subordinates A, B, C, D "must be ordered, must be directed, must be instructed through the marketing manager only", "to avoid the contradiction of orders".
Each worker has one boss. If two managers give a worker opposite orders, whichever he obeys, the other becomes an enemy.
Date: 1916 in the transcript ("110 years ago"); Awad wrote 1915. Unity of command is one of Henri Fayol's principles of management (France, 1916). My fact-check
L1 transcript; Awad notes
Management by consensusالإدارة بالإجماع
"There is no decision to be made and to be issued ... without a 100% yes from all people. If just one opposes, the decision will be stopped."
In Japan a worker can take directions from several managers without conflict, because nothing is decided until everyone agrees. Its doctrine: "success is the responsibility of all; failure is the responsibility of all."
L1 transcript
  • The compiled notes label unity of command "USA/West (1916)", built on individualism and widely applied in Egypt and the US; management by consensus is the Japanese, collectivist system. Abdelaal compiled
  • He said management by consensus was developed in America, but the Americans failed to apply it while the Japanese succeeded. Why? Culture: Japanese culture is collectivist (think Kaizen, continuous improvement; you can name Japanese companies like Toyota but rarely a single Japanese innovator), while American, Egyptian, Arab and British cultures are individualist. L1 transcript
Explain it simply

The same management "rule" works in one culture and fails in another. In an individualist culture people want personal credit, so "everyone must agree" feels slow and nobody owns the result. In a collectivist culture the group comes first, so consensus feels natural. That is why the international manager must study the environment before copying a system from home.

The textbook covers individualism vs collectivism in Hofstede's framework. Textbook pp. 87-92

What he said in class
"Divergences between countries, not only in culture, but also in economic-wise, and political-wise as well, and social-wise as well, all of these will impact all the decisions, all plans, all tasks you are going to perform in each foreign firm."
"This is an American-developed management system, and the American failed to apply it ... But it has been succeeded in many Japanese companies ... the Japanese culture is based on the idea of collectivism. While the American one, and Egyptian one, and Arabic one, and the British one, is mainly based on individualism."
L1 transcript
Why an international manager must be creative (the puzzles)

Right after the Bill or Jane case (should Bill or Jane become marketing manager of an American firm's Saudi subsidiary? told in branch 11) he used puzzles to make one point: if you stick only to the information you are given, you will never reach the right decision. Ask questions, make assumptions, build scenarios. L1 transcript

  • Nine dots: join 9 dots with 3 straight lines without lifting the pen. The dots are like the short case report: staying inside them makes it impossible.
  • How many cubes? Not one: six (each face is a square, each square a cube). "This is creativity."
  • The highest point of a handkerchief: pull it up from its centre. He linked this to الوسطية: the middle is the top ("وكذلك جعلناكم أمة وسطا"), not a weak point between two extremes.
  • How many rectangles in a drawn square? More than you first see.

Abdelaal's compiled notes add the word to avoid: stereotyping التنميط. Judging Jane or Bill by a fixed image instead of asking the questions is exactly what the puzzles warn against. Abdelaal compiled

The Bill or Jane case itself, and how he resolved it, is in the How to solve his cases branch.

What he said in class
"In international business, if you have an opportunity to become an international manager, you are required to be a creative person."
L1 transcript, part 1
Extra from the booklet: the successful global manager, market groups, the strategic approach
Booklet p. 1: the successful manager in global companies (7) (1) a global mindset: "think globally and act locally"; (2) long-term vision; (3) negotiation skills; (4) understanding the national culture of each market; (5) emotional intelligence: "the ability to manage individuals emotionally"; (6) the ability to motivate everyone to excel; (7) the desire and ability to take on burdens and foreign assignments.
Booklet p. 1: 5 groups of international markets (1) advanced economies (USA, Japan, Germany, France); (2) developing economies (Hong Kong, Singapore, Taiwan, South Korea); (3) economies in transition (Hungary, Czech Republic, Poland); (4) emerging economies (Argentina, Brazil, China, India); (5) less developed countries (Middle East, Central Africa, Central America): the poorest and least stable.
Booklet p. 1: what the strategic approach requires (7) flexibility more than size; awareness of "hyper competition"; focus on ideas and the organization's ability to learn; managing non-commercial risks; not expecting stability over time; discovering the opportunities that lead to success; foreign investment and its management.
Booklet p. 1: direct vs indirect foreign investment FDI = a resident entity in one economy gets a lasting interest in an enterprise in another (recorded as FDI at 10% or more ownership); long-term, gives the right to manage. Indirect investment = dealings with no ownership share: exporting, licences, concessions, management contracts. (More in Coming later.)
Memory aid His class version is "direct = own plant or JV; indirect = export". The booklet's is the same idea with ownership as the test (10% or more = direct).

Test yourself

Give his two definitions of international business.
(1) The application of all managerial functions, theories and principles in different environments. (2) Any organization doing business in one or more foreign markets, directly or indirectly.
What is the difference between direct and indirect international business? Give his example.
Indirect: selling abroad without your own operation there, e.g. exporting (Faragalla sold in Sudan). Direct: your own plant, subsidiary or branch abroad, wholly owned or a JV (Faragalla builds a plant in Libya).
State Vernon's definition and his criticism of it.
Six or more foreign markets AND an annual turnover of $100 million. "Completely wrong": the cut-off is arbitrary (what about $99 million?). There is no single accepted definition.
Why did the MIDOR incentive plan fail in the UAE?
Higher standard of living there, so money-based incentives motivate less. Same function (motivation), different environment.
Why did management by consensus succeed in Japan but fail in America?
Culture: Japan is collectivist (success and failure are everyone's responsibility); the US is individualist.

2Kinds of international companies

Once a company crosses the border, people give it different names: multinational, multidomestic, global, transnational. They are not synonyms; each name describes how the company runs its foreign units. Then Prof. Abu Qahf showed the best-known way to classify them: by the mindset of headquarters (ethnocentric, polycentric, regiocentric, geocentric).

The four names: multinational, multidomestic, global, transnational
Multinational corporation (MNC)الشركة متعددة الجنسيات
"A cluster of companies spread in different countries and hold by the headquarters."
A family of companies in several countries, all controlled by one head office (e.g. in the USA or France). Not necessarily worldwide.
L1 transcript; Awad notes
Multidomestic company
"An organization with multicountry affiliates ... where each ... affiliate ... has its own strategies. Its own marketing policies, production policies, human resources management policies, and logistics policies" ... "based on the perceived differences between countries."
Each country unit runs almost like a separate local company, because each country is seen as different. Egypt's unit and Lebanon's unit may have completely different policies.
L1 transcript
Global companyالشركة العالمية / الكونية
"A very large company ... that attempts to standardize, and integrate its own operations, products, marketing activities, marketing policies, HR policies, etc., ... on worldwide basis."
Very large, and does things the same way everywhere, with only minor changes. Coca-Cola, Pepsi (even in chips), McDonald's: "what you are going to eat in the USA is the same you are going to eat in Egypt".
Global does not mean "in one industry": he said Coca-Cola also invests in tourism, hotels and fast food and still standardizes inside each industry. Keep the point; his examples are his own claim (today Coca-Cola is known as a drinks company).
L1 transcript
Transnational corporation (TNC)الشركة عابرة القوميات
"An international firm, just like the multinational. But this terminology has been developed by the United Nations ... instead of using multinational, or foreign firm ... For cultural reasons."
Same kind of firm, a softer name. He said most foreign investment flows from developed countries (the USA, Portugal, Spain, France, Britain) into developing ones, most of which were once occupied, where "foreign" sounds like "colonization". The UN chose "transnational" to avoid that negative image.
L1 transcript
His views

On the UN: "Of course they are fooling people ... It only serves the major countries, and the rest of the countries are victims of the five ... that have the veto right." L1 transcript

Booklet p. 3: another classification (5 types) Multi-local (each branch designs its own strategy for its market) = his "multidomestic"; global (coordinates and integrates operations, products, marketing, finance, HR worldwide: Coca-Cola); international (may be global or multi-local); multinational (a "cluster organization" of companies controlled by one head office); transnational (has the characteristics of the global or the multinational company; new name: "multicultural and multinational companies"). Booklet p. 2 also says the UN prefers "transnational" to reduce the psychological and political effect of "multinational" in developing countries.
Class vs booklet: "transnational"
In class
The same kind of firm as a multinational, under a softer name chosen by the UN.
Booklet p. 3 (and most textbooks)
A distinct type that combines global integration (scale economies) with local responsiveness.

My advice: write his meaning first; add the booklet's as "another view" if the question asks for types.

The global firm's management team: 3 objectives

A global firm needs a global management team with three major objectives: L1 transcript

  1. Search worldwide for opportunities to be exploited (a global vision).
  2. Keep (maintain) a presence in key markets.
  3. Look for similarities among countries to be exploited, e.g. one Arabic advertisement or one product for the 22 Arab countries instead of one per country.

Objective 3 is why global firms enjoy economies of scale: one product for 22 countries means producing 100 million units instead of 1 million. L1 transcript

Memory aid S-K-S: Search, Keep, Similarities (and similarities lead to scale).
What he said in class
"Instead of making an advertisement to Jordan, and another to Egypt, another to Morocco ... just one piece of advertisement in Arabic language will respond to the need ... And this is why these companies are easy to make what is called economies of scale."
L1 transcript
Classifying multinationals: ethnocentric, polycentric, regiocentric, geocentric

MNCs can be classified on many bases (technological, political, technical, nationality). The best-known classification is by headquarters' orientation: L1 transcript

TypeHis meaningOne-line picture
Ethnocentric مركزي / متمركز حول الوطن الأمCentralized: all decisions and strategies are made at headquarters; subsidiaries have no freedom to shape their own strategies."Home knows best."
Polycentric لامركزيDecentralized: each subsidiary formulates its own policies and strategies in production, marketing, everything."Each country knows best."
Regiocentric (regional)Organized by region: "focused on regional integration" (compiled notes)."Each region knows best."
Geocentric جغرافي / عالميA large, integrated company: integrated horizontally, vertically, or both."The world is one system."

Source of the classification: Howard Perlmutter (1969), a management professor at Wharton (USA). His original scheme had three types, E, P and G, and the booklet gives those three. Regiocentric was added later (Heenan and Perlmutter, 1979), which gives "EPRG". Booklet p. 2; general knowledge The textbook uses the same words for staffing policies. Textbook pp. 420-422

Explain it simply

Ask one question: whose way of doing things wins? Ethnocentric: headquarters' way, everywhere (a branch is a copy of home). Polycentric: each country's own way (each branch is almost a local company). Regiocentric: one way per region (one plan for the Gulf, another for Europe). Geocentric: the best way from anywhere, inside one integrated world company. The first one is the easiest to run and the worst at adapting; the second adapts well but is hard to control.

Vertical integrationالتكامل الرأسي
"Upward, I mean toward the market. Downward, toward the raw material."
His example: a spinning and weaving company opens its own garment factory and its own stores (upward, toward the market), or its own sheep or cotton farms (downward, toward raw material).
Upward = toward the customer; downward = toward the raw material. (Textbooks call these forward and backward integration; use his words in his exam.)
L1 transcript
Horizontal integrationالتكامل الأفقي
"The same process, the same operation can be spread out in different places."
The same factory again in Alexandria, Damanhur, Tanta and Marsa Matruh.
L1 transcript
Explain it simply: vertical and horizontal integration

What "integration" means. To integrate means to join things together. A company "integrates" when it grows by taking over more of the work itself, instead of paying other companies to do it. There are two ways to do this. Let's follow one clothes company.

Vertical integration: owning more steps of the same chain. Making a shirt takes a chain of steps: cotton farm, then thread, then cloth, then shirt factory, then shop, then customer. Usually, different companies do different steps. Say our company only weaves cloth: it buys cotton thread from someone else and sells the cloth to someone else. Vertical integration means the company takes over steps above or below it in that chain:

  • Toward the customer: it opens its own shirt factory and its own shops, so it sells directly to people.
  • Toward the raw material: it buys its own cotton farm, so nobody can cut off its supply.

Picture the chain standing up like a ladder. The company climbs up and down its own ladder. That's why it's called vertical.

Horizontal integration: doing the same thing in more places. Here the company doesn't add new steps. It copies the same step somewhere else. Our cloth company has one factory in Alexandria. It opens another cloth factory in Tanta, another in Damanhur and another in Marsa Matruh. It still does exactly the same work, just in more places. Picture factories standing side by side in a row. That's why it's called horizontal.

How this connects to "geocentric". Prof. Abu Qahf described the geocentric company as a very big company whose parts are joined together in these two ways, across many countries. For example, it owns its farms in one country, its factories in several others and its shops around the world, and all of them work as one company.

In one line: vertical means owning more steps of the chain, horizontal means the same step in more places, and in his lecture a geocentric company is a big company that does one or both of these.

What he said in class
"The ethnocentric is representing a centralized firm ... all decisions, all strategies are actually made in the headquarters."
"Polycentric is decentralized. Each subsidiary has its own policies, its own strategies."
"Geocentric is a large company ... characterized by integration ... integrated horizontally, or vertically, or both."
L1 transcript
Booklet p. 2: Perlmutter's patterns and their weaknesses
PatternDescriptionWeakness
Ethnocentric (centralized, single-nationality)Basically a national company with production branches abroad; all main decisions at home head office.Cannot adapt to the host environment.
Polycentric (decentralized)High decentralization and freedom of action in branches; weaker parent control; many owning nationalities.Hard to control the branches.
Geocentric (geographic)Integration and geographic spread worldwide; large, with material, human and technical resources.Influenced by home-country culture, especially early on, and tries to impose it on hosts.
Booklet p. 3: Vernon and Livingstone's three groups Based on degree of integration, nature of activity, type of technology. GI: vertically integrated, high technology, extractive and manufacturing industries. GII: horizontally integrated, high technology, less politically sensitive. GIII: transfer advanced technology to developing hosts through direct investment (Volkswagen making cars in Brazil).
Memory aid Weaknesses in three words each: Ethno = can't adapt; Poly = can't control; Geo = imposes home culture.
Exam link The DBA exam (a final exam on this subject from Alexandria University's doctorate program, shared by Dr. Elsere) asks in its question 3 about the degree of international commitment and the ethnocentric firm's mission, culture and HRM. The model answer is in the Exam corner.
Mission vs strategy (start of lecture 2)

Abdelaal's compiled lecture 2 notes open by separating two words people mix up: Abdelaal compiled

Missionالرسالة
What the company is aiming to be, and why the company is existing (the reason).
The reason the company exists. It answers "why are we here?"
Strategyالاستراتيجية
The different types of paths the company will select to achieve its objectives.
The roads chosen to reach the objectives. It answers "how will we get there?"
Mission = why we exist; strategy = how we reach our objectives; objective = the long-term result (see TQM in branch 9: objective vs target).

Useful for the DBA exam question (see the Exam corner) on the ethnocentric firm's "basic company mission".

Test yourself

Mission vs strategy: what is the difference?
Mission = what the company aims to be and why it exists (the reason). Strategy = the paths it selects to achieve its objectives.
Define a multinational and a global company in his words.
Multinational: a cluster of companies in different countries held (controlled) by the headquarters. Global: a very large company that attempts to standardize and integrate its operations, products, marketing and HR policies on a worldwide basis.
Why did the UN invent the word "transnational"?
For cultural reasons: he said most foreign investment flows from developed countries into developing ones, most of them former colonies, where "foreign" or "multinational" carries the negative image of the colonial era.
What are the three objectives of a global firm's management team?
Search worldwide for opportunities (global vision); keep a presence in key markets; look for similarities among countries to exploit (leading to economies of scale).
Ethnocentric vs polycentric vs geocentric in one line each.
Ethnocentric = centralized at HQ; polycentric = decentralized, each subsidiary sets its own strategy; geocentric = large and integrated (vertically and/or horizontally).
Vertical integration upward and downward: which is which?
Upward = toward the market (own garment factory, own stores). Downward = toward raw materials (own cotton or sheep farms).

3Product and market: can my product travel?

Before any company goes abroad it must answer one strategic question, and Prof. Abu Qahf made it sound almost like a law: can the core of our product be internationalized? To answer it you need two exact definitions (product and market) and the three levels of a product. This branch also holds the "global product" idea from lecture 2 and the three options: think local or global, act local or global.

What is a product? The three levels
Productالمنتج
"The product is anything, tangible or intangible, that has characteristics that satisfy a human need."
Tangible = you can touch it (a pen). Intangible = services, ideas, persons, organizations, impressions: a parliament candidate "markets himself"; you market an impression when you dress your best to meet your fiancé.
A product is defined by the need it satisfies, not by being a physical thing.
L1 transcript

His water example: liquid, no colour, no smell, no taste. Exactly these characteristics make it drinkable and keep us alive ("وجعلنا من الماء كل شيء حي"). L1 transcript

LevelHis wordsMobile phone example (his)
1. Core product المنتج الجوهري"The product why": the function, the benefit you enjoy.To communicate, to connect people.
2. Formal product المنتج الشكليThe features.Size, depth, width, colour, weight.
3. Augmented product المنتج المدعمThe extra services around it.Guarantee, instalments, a free cover.

"By-product" in Awad's circle diagram means the product's secondary functions beside its core function (a phone is for communication; its other functions are by-products), not a by-product of manufacturing. L1 transcript; Awad notes

What he said in class
"The company that is planning to become an international one ... is actually required to answer a strategic question. That is: can the core of our product be internationalized or not? If the answer is yes, go international. If the answer is no, stay home."
"The remaining levels, I mean the formal level and the augmented level, can be changed, minor changed from one country to another country. The instruction on this marker is in English. In an Arab country ... this can be translated into Arabic."
L1 transcript
"If your core can be globalized ... okay go international ... If cannot ... stay local."
L2 transcript
Explain it simply

The core is the reason anyone buys. If people in the new country want that same benefit, you can sell there and adjust the surface (labels, colour, service). If the core benefit itself does not exist there, no amount of surface change will help.

A twist from one of the short discussion examples handed out in lecture 1 (Example 4): the same sewing machine had a different core in different countries (a hobby in the US, a basic need in Nigeria, a status symbol elsewhere), so the promotion had to change. See How to solve his cases.

What is a market? ("The market is not a place")
Marketالسوق
"A group of people ... sized by tens, or millions, or billions ... with needs to satisfy, and desire to buy, and they have purchasing power."
Three conditions: a need, a desire to buy, and money (purchasing power). Missing any one, no market.
"The market is not a place." Two students bought the same pen, one in Al-Agami and one in Borg El Arab: same market, different places.
L1 transcript
Memory aid N-D-P: Need, Desire, Purchasing power (people, not a place).
The global product and the three "think / act" options

Because competition is now worldwide, a company must adopt a global perspective. "The key success in a world of growing tendency toward internationalization is ... the development of what can be called a global product." L2 transcript

Global product
"A product that can be marketed worldwide ... mainly based on satisfying customer needs on a worldwide basis."

Test yourself

Define "product" and give its three levels.
Anything, tangible or intangible, that has characteristics that satisfy a human need. Levels: core (the "why", function/benefit), formal (features), augmented (extra services: guarantee, instalments, free cover).
Define "market". Why is it "not a place"?
A group of people (tens to billions) with needs to satisfy, desire to buy and purchasing power. The same pen is bought in different places by the same market.
What strategic question must a firm answer before going international?
Can the core of our product be internationalized? Yes: go international. No: stay home. Formal and augmented levels can get minor local changes.
Name the three think/act options.
Think local act local (domestic); think global act local; think global act global (fully standardized).

4Globalization: a fact or a myth?

Everyone says "the world has become a small village". Prof. Abu Qahf calls that "junk", "a joke": globalization is a big myth. Not because nothing has changed, but because people mix up three different things: the concept itself (free movement of everything, no restrictions), the forces pushing toward it (world trade agreements such as GATT for goods and GATS for services, and technology), and its surface symptoms (burgers, jeans, Coca-Cola). Keep those three apart and his whole argument becomes easy.

Two definitions of globalization
Definition 1: free mobilityالعولمة: حرية الانتقال
"The free mobility of everything between countries without any restrictions": of people, products, services, capital, wealth, technology, scientific research results, "even poverty, even problems".
If anything at all needs permission to cross a border, this definition is not met.
L1 and L2 transcripts
Definition 2: integration
"The tendency toward integrating the world ... on economic basis ... political basis ... and cultural basis" (in lecture 1: "the international integration of goods, services, technology, labor, capital ... on worldwide basis").
The world working as one economy, one political space and one culture.
L1 and L2 transcripts

In lecture 1 he called free mobility (definition 1) "the scientific definition", "a very simple definition" and "the core of globalization". In lecture 2 he introduced integration with "scientifically speaking" and then called free mobility "maybe much easier". Either way, definition 1 is the one he builds his "myth" argument on. L1, L2 transcripts The textbook's version: "the trend toward greater economic, cultural, political, and technological interdependence among national institutions and economies". Textbook p. 31

Booklet p. 6: how the booklet sees globalization "Globalization is colonialism in a new garment made in the United States", also Westernization; it does not respect the individual's intellectual integrity or national identity, and assumes cultures will not survive. Its principles: market fundamentalism ("if the commodity does not fit the market, the market will be modified to fit the commodity", so globalization is "a trap for consumption"); one-sided utilitarianism (النفعية: judging everything only by the benefit or profit it brings); the individual as an economic, not cultural, unit; similarity of tastes and the media; consumerist materialism. Distances die through communications, "but distances do not die from the geopolitical or geostrategic point of view, and the comprehensive power of the world springs from diversity, not from standardization". This matches his "death of distance" point (next sub-branch).
Booklet p. 1: economic globalization depends on (7) information technology and the Internet; companies' social and ethical responsibility; a global product or global customer; global business standards and products; growth of trade, investment and their agreements; new competitors from emerging economies; the fading of borders.
Why it is a myth: the evidence

Test definition 1 against real life. Nothing moves freely: L1, L2 transcripts

  • People: you need a visa for Saudi Arabia, France, Britain or the USA. The USA restricted Mahmoud Abbas from going to the UN General Assembly.
  • Products: the EU sets its own standards. A charger carries the CE mark (certified to European standards); without it, it can "never ever" enter the EU.
  • Blocs are not globalization: the EU is an agreement among accepted countries only; outside it, you still need a visa.
  • Disputes everywhere: USA and Iran, Iran and the Gulf, Egypt and Ethiopia, Algeria and Morocco, Afghanistan, Kashmir. "To talk about a tendency toward unification of the world, nonsense."
  • Research results, technology, innovation do not move freely either.

His rule: "As long as there are restrictions, don't talk about globalization." "As long as you have 'no', you will have also a big 'myth'." L1 transcript

The death of distance
"We are living in the death of distance ... rather than globalization."
Transport and communication make it feel close: a flight to the USA in 8-10 hours, an easy call to a friend in the USA, Saudi Arabia in a couple of hours instead of weeks by camel. But geographic distance and cultural differences are still the same. "The world will never ever become a small village or just one market."
Easier contact is the death of distance, not globalization.
Explain it simply

His test is strict on purpose: globalization means everything moves freely. So one visa, one standard, one border check is enough to say "not yet". What we really see is that travel and talk have become fast and cheap. That makes the world feel smaller, but the borders, the rules and the cultural differences are still there.

The 4 indicators (types) of globalization (from the booklet only, not taught in lectures 1-3; asked in past papers): Booklet p. 7

IndicatorSigns
Globalization of demand عولمة الطلبThe same product offered to different geographic segments; local demand added up into global demand. Examples: jeans, fast-food restaurants, Pepsi and Coca-Cola (his "superficial symptoms").
Globalization of supply عولمة العرضNew international division of labour; specialization in making components; fast movement of production factors; subcontracting; concentrated R&D; technology exchange (USA, EU, Japan).
Globalization of competition عولمة المنافسةFrom comparative to competitive advantage (from a country's natural edge, such as cheap labour or raw materials, to an edge firms build, such as quality, brand or technology); from local to international competitiveness; fast spread of booms and recessions; strategic alliances.

Scale vs scope: economies of scale = cheaper per unit because you make more of one product; economies of scope = cheaper because you make several related products with the same resources.

Memory aid Indicators D-S-C-S: Demand, Supply, Competition, Strategy ("Don't Sell Cheap Stuff").
Booklet p. 7: driving, conditional and governing factors

Driving forces (8): the information-technology revolution; GATT and trade-liberalization talks; the end of the Cold War; progress in transport, communication and printing; sudden global problems (pollution, AIDS, Covid-19); poor countries cannot be sources of flows to rich ones; wealth concentrated in a few countries and MNC dominance; a UN environment that lets America act as "the world's policeman".

Conditional factors (5) العوامل الشرطية: the retreat of the state's power; US efforts to break up big countries (the Soviet Union); widespread belief that globalization is inevitable; the belief that everything ("things and non-things") can be globalized; globalization needs national culture to be negated.

Governing factors: the centres of globalization pressing Third World countries: debt, forced sale of assets, exporting only raw materials, aid that supports consumption, threats of force or sanctions (Iraq).

Centres: North America, the EU, the Far East (Japan; now also China and South Korea).

Booklet p. 8: is there a theory of globalization? No. Reasons include: it is a phenomenon, and a phenomenon is not permanent; its governing principle is utilitarianism (النفعية: judging everything only by the benefit or profit it brings), which leads to "market fundamentalism" (the market and profit rule everything) or "economic barbarism"; it leads to alienation and loss of freedom; it conflicts with liberalism and diversity; and glocalization (global + local: a global firm giving its products a local character): Ford, Coca-Cola and McDonald's standardize, while Toyota lets the consumer decide what is produced. Confronting globalization: regionalism (regional blocs) and nationalization / localization الوطننة, which "is not a war on globalization" (booklet p. 7).

How to hold MNCs accountable (booklet p. 8) is in Coming later.

Agreements between developed and developing nations "ensure equal opportunities ... but never ever secure equal results". L2 transcript

Signing GATT and GATS was "the big crime committed worldwide" against third-world countries. The blame is on the government that signed without asking the other side to help develop its production factors to meet their standards. L2 transcript

Story: the Egyptian undershirts in England

In an English mall he found 100% Egyptian cotton undershirts made by Gil (Alexandria), expensive. He bought 4, a colleague bought the rest, a third man came and found none. The shop ordered Egyptian cotton shirts from Egypt. They arrived by sea; the humidity rusted the pins, spoiled the shirts, and the order was rejected. By air, or with decent pins, it would have worked. His word for it: الغباء (stupidity). L2 transcript
