Result (Figure 3-2): as the error rate fell, so did the cost. "Quality and cost are inversely related!" Firms missed it because they were "blind-sided by the old quality/cost paradox". Handout Ch3 p. 68

Class graph vs handout Same idea, two drawings. In class: cost of quality control against defective units, engineers (traditional) vs managers (modern). In the handout: Figure 3-1 = the engineers' old assumption, Figure 3-2 = the research result (the managers' view). In an exam, draw either and name Motorola and six sigma.
Memory aid Engineers count today's bill; managers count tomorrow's customer.
Modern example Toyota's lean production (built-in quality, stopping the line at a defect) is the classic case for the managers' view: quality built in early costs less than fixing defects later.
Technology paradox, the innovation challenge, and "quality pays off"

From the handout only (not in the class notes). Handout Ch3 p. 69-75

The technology paradox
"High-tech MNCs can thrive at the very moment their prices are falling the fastest." George Fisher (Motorola, then Kodak): "The only thing that matters is if the exponential growth of your market is faster than the exponential decline of your prices."
Old belief: be first to market and charge premium prices. New belief: cut prices as fast as possible, win world market share, and make the money on the follow-on market (spinoff products). Toshiba will not earn back its digital-movie player, but will on spinoffs (audio players, laptop storage). Teleport installs fiber with 1 million times the capacity needed, free, because the customer will grow into it.
Handout Ch3 p. 69-70

So successful MNCs build a technology architecture: one technology that feeds a series of related products and markets (cheap DRAM chips, then Windows "gobbles megabytes of DRAMs"). PC makers add software, troubleshooting and training so the PC is not a generic product sold on price; Dell tailors machines to each customer (mass customization). Handout Ch3 p. 70

The innovation challenge Handout Ch3 p. 70-71

Michael Porter: the key to winning global battles is the ability to innovate continually. 3M earns 30% of its revenue from products less than 4 years old, uses databases that give staff "bureaucracy-free access" to experts, brings in outside experts, has scientists present to peers, keeps customers in view at every stage, and uses cross-functional teams: "Managers must set goals, then get out of the way." Three approaches to stimulate innovation:

  1. Having a vision of the future market: Canon imagined small, cheap copiers everywhere; Harley-Davidson executives go to biker rallies; Epson's young engineers spend 6 months in sales and 6 in service.
  2. Benchmarking, even against yourself: Raychem replaced its own $125 million telephone-cable splice product with a better one, so rivals copying the old one had to start again.
  3. Product proliferation: so many versions that competitors cannot copy fast enough, and customers buy from the firm with the most choice. Canon planned its second-generation copier before the first left the line.
Memory aid Innovation V-B-P: Vision, Benchmarking, Proliferation.

Quality pays off: three examples Handout Ch3 p. 72-75

  • Autos (J.D. Power, 1995): GM 0.99, Ford 1.14, Chrysler 1.37 defects per car; Honda Prelude 0.48, Lexus LS 400 0.51. US strategies: start from scratch (Saturn) or replace old models (Lumina, Cavalier).
  • Aircraft: Boeing's quality won orders for over 30 of its 777 stretch jet (777-300X) from five Asian airlines; Airbus and McDonnell Douglas also won orders "based on proven track records".
  • Asian services: Malaysian, Singaporean and Thai airlines and Shangri-La and Mandarin Oriental hotels top service polls. Services' share of GDP grew (Figure 3-3); Hong Kong's manufacturing workers fell from 1.5 million (1980) to about 600,000 (1995). Asian services trade rose almost 300% in 10 years; Thailand, the Philippines and India opened banking and telephones to foreign firms.

Lesson: "if countries close themselves to outside competition, they will be unable to compete worldwide", because they become isolated and fail to develop state-of-the-art goods and services. Handout Ch3 p. 74-75

Box: "Where's the Quality Service in Deutschland?" Germans are seen as efficient, but not in services. Deutsche Telekom, the phone monopoly: a woman waited 23 years for a phone in old East Germany; DT has 62.6 employees per 10,000 lines (NTT 42.4, US Baby Bells 43.2). BASF switched its international calls to British Telecom and saves 15-60% per call; ordinary Germans have no choice and make only 600 calls a year (Americans over 3 times that). Now the monopoly is ending and DT runs a massive TQM effort. Handout Ch3 p. 74
Explain it simply

Two "paradoxes" that are not really contradictions. Quality: better quality looks more expensive, but fewer defects means less waste, so it ends up cheaper. Technology: cutting your price looks like losing money, but a cheap product spreads fast and you earn on everything that comes after it, like printers sold cheaply and ink sold dearly.

The Xerox case: how Japan's copiers forced a quality revolution

Elsere's note: Japanese manufacturers disrupted US competitors (Xerox) by substituting metal components with plastic parts (he wrote 90%, possibly 50%), cutting manufacturing cost while keeping high quality. Elsere p. 8

Booklet p. 17 Xerox grew for years on photocopiers; then it licensed others, its patents aged, and Japanese firms entered with lower production costs. The CEO faced two challenges: recover lost market share and rebuild staff morale. He launched "Leadership through Quality" and used benchmarking (reference frameworks) to involve employees and improve quality: (1) a competitor: bought a rival copier, took it apart and costed every part; (2) a non-competitor in supply and logistics: L.L. Bean (a US outdoor-clothing mail-order retailer); (3) handling and distribution: Kodak. Lesson (booklet p. 18 MCQs): benchmarks can come from inside or outside your industry, or both.
Pillars 2 and 3: the learning organization and the World Class Organization

In class (lecture 3) he only named these two strategies; the details come from the booklet (below) and from the lecture 4 handout (the next two sub-branches, which are fuller). L3 transcript

Booklet p. 19: learning organization The ability to transform and develop through learning and adaptation (also called transformational leadership); the review sheet adds: anticipating change and finding new ways to innovate (past-exam p. 10). Three requirements: (1) creation, creativity and innovation; (2) openness; (3) individuals' learning and self-confidence. "Learning organizations are organizations able to adapt and improve continuously."
Booklet p. 19: World Class Organization (WCO) The elite class of world companies (examples given: Sony, Kodak, Honda, Xerox), able to compete anywhere, any time, against anyone, in any way. Six pillars: (1) orientation to customers' needs; (2) continuous improvement to cut cost and raise quality; (3) flexible organization and attention to supply sources; (4) creative human-resource management; (5) a work climate of justice and equality; (6) technological and IT support.
Booklet p. 19: pillars of competitive advantage Using local components; a network of local relationships, people's learning and a good reputation; narrowing the gap between customers' expectations and what can be produced; transferring knowledge.
Booklet p. 16: innovation Innovation is "the permanent challenge" for MNCs. Firms raise innovation and quality by attracting outside experts and supporting scientists, encouraging innovations with a special vision, and using reference frameworks (benchmarking).
Memory aid Learning organization C-O-L: Creativity, Openness, Learning and self-confidence.
The learning organization: class (lecture 4) and handout
Learning organization (class)
"A company is able to adapt and [improve] continuous[ly]": learning organization = adaptation + continuous improvement.
Improvement, not development: improvement = small changes; development = huge changes. A learning company keeps making small steps.
L4 notes (Ahmed)
  1. Self-efficacy is connected to empowerment: encourage people to think and to create.
  2. Openness is a systems view: inputs → operation → outputs. Inputs = environmental variables (political, economic, cultural) + laws + labour + machines + ... If the output is satisfactory, fine; if not, reconsider the inputs or the operation. "Openness is information": companies die from a lack of information or poor-quality information (red flag 11, branch 10).
  3. Creativity = newness: "to get something new where there is no previous example of it". Creativity is the ideation component of innovation, so innovation is the application of creativity. "Innovation is not canned ideas." His example: the Giza pyramid is creative work, because it is (1) new, (2) without a previous example, and (3) it passes the time test.
Memory aid Class triangle C-O-S: Creativity, Openness, Self-efficacy (= the handout's personal efficacy, the booklet's self-confidence).

The handout's fuller version

Adaptive vs learning organization
Adaptive organizations "are characterized by reaction to required changes but a failure to anticipate and stay on or ahead of the cutting edge." "A learning organization is able to transform itself by anticipating change and discovering new ways of creating products and services; it has learned how to learn."
Many MNCs reach quality and then slip back because they were too slow or did not see the change coming. The adaptive firm reacts; the learning firm anticipates. Examples: Motorola and Sony; Kodak under George Fisher moving from silver film to digital imaging; Gruppo GFT (the world's largest designer-clothing maker) designing for local differences instead of standardized world apparel.
Handout Ch3 p. 78

Three characteristics of learning organizations: openness, creativity, personal efficacy. Handout Ch3 p. 78

  1. Openness: not only accept new trends but "encourage and anticipate changes"; learn to accommodate, create and profit from change; suspend the need to control everything; empower associates, flatten the structure, allow flexibility, re-examine core values. Whirlpool: saw the US would no longer be its biggest market; vision of "growing a transnational company"; all senior managers with global experience by 2000; joint venture with Philips in Europe, others in India and Mexico; a 1990 Montreux conference of 140 managers; 15 cross-national-functional teams for a "one company" culture. Handout Ch3 p. 78-79
  2. Creativity, with two aspects: personal flexibility (Emerson, GE and RCA expected radio sales to mature and decline; flexible Sony changed the product life cycle with the Walkman) and willingness to take risks (Japanese automakers and Chrysler both found no support for minivans in US market research; Chrysler took the risk anyway and earned record profits). Handout Ch3 p. 79-80
  3. Personal efficacy: "the belief that one both can and should learn to influence significantly the world in which one lives". Built by self-awareness (a clear vision plus feedback; "information seeking"; Whirlpool's 360-degree evaluations from self, peers, subordinates and bosses, focused on potential, with feedback usually to the person only) and proactive problem-solving (IBM stopped waiting for surveys and now calls customers who left, to find out why and win them back). Handout Ch3 p. 80-81
Booklet vs handout Booklet p. 19: creativity and innovation; openness; individuals' learning and self-confidence. Handout: openness, creativity, personal efficacy. The same three: "personal efficacy" is the handout's name for learning and self-confidence. Write the handout names and add the booklet wording in brackets.
Memory aid O-C-E: "Open, Creative, Efficacious" (all three words also appear in the Generative column of Table 3-1).

Box: "Bit Players Bite the Dust" Thousands of small Japanese suppliers went out of business. They had borrowed heavily in the early 1990s to upgrade for their big customers; when the yen rose, Toyota, Nissan and Sony demanded lower prices or switched to cheap offshore suppliers (Ricoh now imports 10% of its parts from China and other low-cost places, up from 2%). One lens maker fell from 5,000 lenses a month to under 2,000. Survivors hold sophisticated niches with little competition, but "they must become learning organizations". Handout Ch3 p. 80
The World-Class Organization: class (5 points) and the handout's 6 pillars

In class: "When a company applies TQM and L.O., the company is now qualified to be a world class organization" (the "club"). A world-class organization: L4 notes (Ahmed)

  1. is customer oriented (customer-based focus);
  2. has creative human resources management: a new incentive system, promotion, gathering talents, healthy work conditions, the salary system;
  3. uses modern or advanced technology;
  4. looks after its suppliers ("more interest"). "It is not risky to assume that the success of any company starts with its supplier": suppliers can save you time and inventory cost, and advise you. Example: a pharmacy, where the supplier collects only after the pharmacy sells;
  5. has justice in the working climate: "no production with injustice".
Class 5 vs handout and booklet 6 The class list has 5 of the 6 pillars: customer (1), HRM (4), technology (6), suppliers (= flexible or virtual organization and global sourcing, 3), justice (= egalitarian climate, 5). Missing in class: continuous improvement (2), which he had put under the learning organization. Write the 6 and use his supplier and justice wording as examples.

The handout's 6 pillars

World-class organization (WCO)
"World-class organizations (WCOs) are enterprises that are able to compete with anybody, anywhere, anytime, anyway."
Most operate worldwide (Motorola, Sony, Hewlett-Packard, Kodak, Honda, Xerox); a few focus on one region but still beat all comers, foreign or domestic (Ritz-Carlton, Wainwright Industries, Wal-Mart). The pillars work "in both an additive and synergistic way", a level beyond TQM and the learning organization.
Handout Ch3 p. 81
  1. Customer-based focus: know internal and external customers; flat structures so everyone is close to the customer; go beyond satisfying to delight and bond; create new demand (Sony Walkman). Wal-Mart broke the old push model and built a pull system (customers pull goods off the shelf); so do Metro (Germany), Ito-Yokado (Japan), Carrefour (France). Handout Ch3 p. 81-82
  2. Continuous improvement (CI): improve faster, more efficiently and more effectively than rivals. Ford cut vendor-payment processing time by 90% by cutting sign-offs; Motorola cut order processing from almost 11 days to 2.7 (auto-approval of credit of $5,000 or less, all entries computerized). Handout Ch3 p. 82
  3. Fluid, flexible or virtual organization: "able to conduct business as if it were a very large enterprise ... while in fact it is much smaller, made up of core business competencies with the rest outsourced". The tool is global sourcing: "the use of worldwide suppliers, regardless of where they are located geographically, who are best able to provide the needed output". But home-based suppliers are preferred where possible (Porter: close links speed innovation), and suppliers follow big customers (Ford's US suppliers set up near its new European plants). Handout Ch3 p. 83
  4. Creative HRM: people are the most important asset; "knowledge-based organizations are replacing traditional asset-based MNCs". Empowered teams (Ritz-Carlton staff can spend up to $1,000 on a guest problem); suggestion systems (Wainwright: 55 suggestions per employee a year, against 12 at typical Japanese firms and 0.3 at typical US firms); training (Samsung, South Korea's largest chaebol (conglomerate): a year-long program abroad for over 1,000 middle managers at over $80,000 each, "goof around and learn"); open, publicized rewards (Ritz-Carlton "First Class" cards, "Lightning Strikes" cash awards, dinners for the best ideas). Handout Ch3 p. 83-84
  5. Egalitarian climate: all stakeholders (employees, customers, owners, suppliers, community) "treated with dignity and respect". Wal-Mart calls everyone an "associate"; a Ritz-Carlton associate escorts a guest instead of pointing. Suppliers become part of the team instead of being played off against each other (IBM brings suppliers into product design; Sony and Mitsubishi cost the product with them). Handout Ch3 p. 84-85
  6. Technological support: CAD/CAM, telecom networks, expert systems, MIS. Retail: Wal-Mart's just-in-time inventory; Tesco cut stock in its chain to 2 weeks (aiming at 1) and forecasts from point-of-sale data, and can now buy from one small cheese maker for one store in York; The Limited's EDI with Hong Kong makers cut order-to-delivery from 9 months to 5 weeks; Marks and Spencer tracks suppliers by EDI. Handout Ch3 p. 85-86
Memory aid C-C-F-H-E-T: "Clever Companies Find Happy Equal Technology": Customer, Continuous improvement, Flexible/virtual, HRM, Egalitarian, Technology.

The chapter's last word: "If MNCs do not become world class, they may not survive in the long run." This links straight to branch 10, why companies die. Handout Ch3 p. 86

Sustaining world class: his 18 ways (lecture 4) and the booklet's 20 mechanisms

"It is easy for a company to be a world class, but not easy to sustain or maintain global competitiveness and develop it." So, how to sustain and develop world class (ways, tools, strategies, policies): L4 notes (Ahmed)

  1. Continuous R&D to get new products and to improve existing ones (higher quality or cheaper), maybe with new technology; also improve production methods and technology; a higher degree of efficiency.
  2. A good database: managers need data and information to make effective decisions; the quality, quantity and timing of information matter.
  3. A new product attached to the existing one ("like a mobile cover"): it adds value and creates business.
  4. Customer intimacy: manage his expectations, let him participate, put yourself in his shoes, respond to his needs.
  5. Continuous value added to the customer: write the best use on the packaging, follow up, advise him. All this builds customer retention: attracting a new customer costs double keeping one.
  6. New sources and techniques to deal with the market and the customer.
  7. Strategic alliances and joint ventures, for instance with a supplier, a retailer or a wholesaler.
  8. Global partnership with global firms.
  9. Form a global team.
  10. Capitalize on the waves of generations: win today's customer and the next generation at the same time. His childhood story: his grandfather sent him to buy tobacco from "Uncle El-Sayed", who gave the boy a bonbon every time, so the boy loved going back. The grandfather trusted the merchant, and the clever merchant made the young generation love him: tomorrow's customers.
  11. Simplicity: "is always winning".
  12. One promise kept: six selling appeals with five fulfilled are worse than one selling appeal that is fulfilled.
  13. Invest in marketing.
  14. Speed: in responding to the customer, in entering the market, "speed for everything".
  15. Diversify the weapons to attack competitors: the more cards (merits, advantages) a company holds, the greater its potential to beat the others.
  16. Grasp the competitors' factors of success.
  17. Continuous audit of everything: production, marketing, every activity.
  18. Smile.
Customer retention, not "customer loyalty"
"Customer loyalty is an old school term: no loyal customers. Recently it's called customer retention."
No customer is loyal; each one follows his own interest. So you keep him by serving his interest better, and by understanding him better than your competitors do.
L4 notes (Ahmed)
His 18 vs the booklet's 20 Almost the same list in a different order. Class number = booklet number: 1 = 6 + 7; 2 = 5; 3 = 8; 4 = 1 + 3; 5 = 9 (+ 4); 6 = 15; 7 = 11 (+ 2); 8 = 19; 9 = 16; 10 = 17; 11 and 14 = 10 (simplicity, speed); 12 and 13 = 20 (+ 12); 15 and 16 = 14; 17 is close to 13 (continuous review). Only in class: smile. Only in the booklet: a supportive organizational structure (18). In the exam write his 18; "a supportive structure" can be a 19th.
Memory aid for his 18 Group them: Product (1 R&D, 3 add-on product), Information (2 database, 17 audit), Customer (4 intimacy, 5 value added, 6 new techniques, 12 one promise, 18 smile), Partners (7 alliances, 8 global partners, 9 global team), Market (10 generations, 13 marketing, 14 speed, 11 simplicity), Competitors (15 weapons, 16 their success factors).

The booklet's 20 mechanisms Booklet p. 24

Booklet p. 24
  1. Embrace the customer and respond fast.
  2. Partner with suppliers; offer product alternatives.
  3. Let customers share in decisions.
  4. Understand the customer before competitors do.
  5. Accurate information and an information base.
  6. Continuous R&D to develop the product at the lowest cost.
  7. Continuous research to improve production methods and control cost.
  8. Produce goods that accompany and complement the main product.
  9. Keep adding value for customers.

  11. Strategic alliances with suppliers, distributors and supporting bodies.
  12. Keep promises to customers, without over-promising.
  13. Continuously review the challenges of the international environment.

Test yourself

What are the "4 any's"?
Compete any time, anywhere, any way, against anybody.
Name the 3 pillar strategies and the 4 TQM requirements.
TQM, learning organization, World Class Organization. TQM: quality vision, product diversification, employee empowerment, benchmarking.
Objective vs target: what is the difference?
Objective = long-term result (business continuity); target / aim / goal = short-term result (immediate profit).
Explain the quality-cost graph and the two views.
More spending on quality control means fewer defective units (7,000 EGP: 50 defects; 9,000: 30). Managers (modern view): quality spending saves ultimate cost and keeps customers. Engineers (traditional): it raises upfront cost.
What did Xerox benchmark against?
A competitor's copier (taken apart and costed), L.L. Bean (logistics, a non-competitor) and Kodak (handling and distribution), under "Leadership through Quality".
What does a learning organization need (booklet)?
Creativity and innovation; openness; individuals' learning and self-confidence.
What did Motorola discover about quality and cost (sigma)?
The old "bath tub" belief said cost explodes as failures approach zero. Measuring defects per million (3 sigma 66,810 down to 6 sigma 3.4), Motorola found that as errors fell, so did cost: quality and cost are inversely related (Figures 3-1 and 3-2).
What is the technology paradox?
High-tech MNCs can thrive while their prices fall fastest: cut prices to win market share and profit from the follow-on market (Toshiba, Teleport). Fisher: market growth must beat price decline.
Three approaches to stimulate innovation (handout)?
Having a vision (Canon, Harley-Davidson, Epson), benchmarking even against yourself (Raychem), product proliferation (Canon).
Handout: the 3 characteristics of total quality MNCs, and the 3 of learning organizations?
TQM: vision formulation, empowerment, benchmarking. Learning: openness, creativity (flexibility, risk-taking), personal efficacy (self-awareness, proactive problem-solving).
Adaptive vs learning organization?
Adaptive reacts to change but fails to anticipate it; learning anticipates change and has learned how to learn (Table 3-1: better sameness vs meaningful difference, market share vs market creation, bureaucratic vs network).
Lecture 4: what makes a learning organization, and its 3 requirements?
Adaptation + continuous improvement (improvement = small changes, not development = huge changes). Requirements: creativity / innovation, openness, self-efficacy. Openness = inputs, operation, outputs: if the output is not satisfactory, reconsider the inputs or the operation.
Creativity vs innovation (class)?
Creativity = newness, something new with no previous example; it is the ideation component of innovation. Innovation = the application of creativity, "not canned ideas". Example: the Giza pyramid (new, no previous example, passes the time test).
Name 10 of his 18 ways to sustain world class.
Continuous R&D; a good database; an add-on product; customer intimacy; continuous value added (retention); new techniques for the market; strategic alliances and JVs; global partnership; a global team; capitalize on generations; simplicity; one fulfilled selling appeal; invest in marketing; speed; diversify weapons; grasp competitors' success factors; continuous audit; smile.
Why "customer retention" and not "customer loyalty"?
He calls loyalty an old-school term: there are no loyal customers, each follows his own interest. Retention is kept by adding value and understanding him better than competitors; a new customer costs double an existing one.
The 6 WCO pillars, one example each?
Customer focus (Wal-Mart pull), continuous improvement (Motorola 11 to 2.7 days), virtual organization and global sourcing (Ford's suppliers), creative HRM (Ritz-Carlton $1,000, Wainwright 55 suggestions, Samsung training), egalitarian climate (Wal-Mart associates, IBM suppliers), technological support (Tesco, The Limited EDI).

10Why companies die (Richard Watson)

Branch 9 showed the companies that survive. In the same lecture Prof. Abu Qahf asked the opposite question: why do companies die, and can we see it coming? He quoted a study by Richard Watson (a British writer on future trends): out of 500 American companies only 25 will still be in the market by 2027. Then he gave the warning signs, and our classmate Dr. Elsere's notes list 12 of them as "red flags" that executives must watch. Each one is easy to remember if you picture the company it describes.

The study he quoted

"A very extensive and comprehensive analysis and study of 600 global or international companies: 500 American and 100 British ... conducted in 2017 ... By the year 2027 ... 25 companies of the 500 American companies will stay in the market ... the 475 will be out of the market. Out of 100 British companies only 24 will stay in the market." L3 transcript; Elsere p. 5

Elsere's framing: empirical research such as Watson's study of 600 British and American firms "indicates high long-term corporate failure rates for organizations that fail to continuously modernize these strategic pillars" (TQM, learning organization, WCO). So company death is the opposite of global competitiveness. Elsere p. 5

Found online Richard Watson (a UK futurist) wrote "Why Companies Die" (What's Next: Top Trends blog, 13 March 2016). It cites Richard Foster (Yale): the average lifespan of an S&P 500 company (the 500 largest US listed firms) fell from 67 years in the 1920s to 15 years, and about 75% of S&P 500 firms will be gone by around 2027; of the FTSE 100 companies of 1984 (the 100 largest UK listed firms), only 24 were still around in 2012. Its reasons: mergers and takeovers, failing to react to new technology, customers or business models, complacency after success, new ideas rejected by a "corporate immune system", slow reaction to visible warnings, short-termism. The article does not mention "2017" or "600 companies". In his exam, use his numbers. Online: Watson 2016, toptrends.nowandnext.com
The 12 red flags of corporate failure

"Executive leadership must monitor 12 critical operational red flags that predict corporate decline and failure." Elsere pp. 5-7

#Red flagWhat it looks like
1High turnover of skilled personnelSkilled staff resign (relative to unskilled). Who will run the company then? The unskilled, and "unskilled people will lead to the death".
2Under-investment in marketingToo little money for marketing. He: "marketing expenditure actually representing investment": campaigns, developing salespeople, new products with production.
3Failure in customer acquisitionNo new customers over a 6-month period.
4Ineffective after-sales servicesPoor post-purchase support degrades customer trust.
5Slow new product developmentNo new product (or size or colour variation) within a 12-month window.
6Refusal of new ideas and innovationActive rejection of disruptive concepts (Kodak, Nokia).
7Excess inventory and marketing myopiaLarge stock piles with low turnover; high holding costs from producing beyond demand. (Marketing myopia = short-sightedness: looking at your own product instead of at what customers want.)
8Lack of strategic planning and board agingNo product planning; no ambitious, young leaders on the board.
9Single-source dependency (low external flexibility)Over-reliance on one supplier, one customer or one manpower source.
10Organizational hypocrisy النفاقFlattering employees feed false or misleading information to senior executives.
11Inefficient information systemsPoor management information (timing and quality) undermines decisions.
12Internal governance conflictsDestructive personal conflicts among owners, partners or major shareholders.
Memory aid Group the 12 into four stories: People leave and fight (1, 8, 10, 12); Customers are neglected (2, 3, 4); Products get stale (5, 6, 7); Weak links (9, 11). Or remember the order in class: skilled people, marketing, customers in 6 months.

On hypocrisy he said: "Lie is very dangerous." Abdelaal compiled

The transcript records only the first three in detail (after-sales service comes up inside no. 3), then jumps to the quality graph; the notes complete the list. Abdelaal's notes list 10 (no information systems; single-source dependency treated with the ratio below).

Explain it simply

Each red flag is a symptom you can see from outside long before the company closes: good people leave, money for marketing is cut, no new customers, no new products, stock piling up, flattery instead of truth, owners fighting. One flag is a warning; several together mean the company is dying. Watch for them in your own company too.

Why do skilled people resign? (class discussion) L3 transcript

Low salary; a bad salary or incentive system; no promotion chances; injustice and unequal treatment; bad leadership and supervision; poor physical working conditions (electricity, water, air); wanting their own business; a different passion. "I can suggest an endless list of reasons."

Why can't a firm win new customers? L3 transcript

High price, bad quality, price above what buyers expect, weak promotion (people don't know the product), bad sales and after-sales service. After-sales service also decides customer retention.

What he said in class
"The resignation of skilled people in a certain company represent one of the most important criteria through which to predict this company will never ever stay in the market."
"If the company couldn't attract new customers during six months, this company will get out of the market."
L3 transcript
The external flexibility ratio (a worked example)
External flexibility ratioنسبة المرونة الخارجية
(Single supplier / total suppliers) x 100
How much of your buying (or selling) depends on one partner. A higher ratio means a lower degree of flexibility: the supplier controls the company.
Elsere p. 7
SupplierABCDETotal
Purchases100,0001,0003,0001,0001,000106,000

Ratio for A = 100,000 / 106,000 x 100 = 94.3% (Elsere also labels it the "interdependency ratio"). A supplies almost everything, so if A stops, the company stops. "Dependency on one supplier or customer = high risk of corporate death." Elsere p. 7

Two notes, two numbers
Elsere's notes
D = 1,000; total 106,000; ratio for A = 94.3%.
Abdelaal's compiled notes
D = 5,000; total 110,000; ratio for A = 100,000 / 110,000 = 90.9% (he calls it the "dependency ratio").

Both are arithmetically right; they read supplier D differently from the board. The method is what matters: single supplier divided by total, times 100; higher ratio = less flexibility.

The booklet's 20 indicators (from earlier batches)
Booklet p. 23 Essay question "indicators for predicting the death of global companies according to Richard Watson":
  1. Resignation of competent staff and management cadres.
  2. No new customers within 6 months.
  3. Shrinking average sales to loyal customers.
  4. Falling profits reinvested in the company.
  5. No new products within 6 months to a year.

11How to solve his cases

Prof. Abu Qahf gives cases in almost every lecture, and he told the class plainly what disappointed him: "most of you summarizes the report. And then try to touch to answer the questions." Too general. Here is the method he asked for, the way he resolved the Bill or Jane case (which of two candidates should run marketing for an American firm's Saudi subsidiary), and the lessons from the four case pages handed out in lecture 1.

Rule 1: the given facts are never enough (ask, assume, build scenarios)

"If you stick to this information or to this report, you will never ever realize the right decision." You must collect more information, ask questions, make assumptions, and develop different scenarios, then choose the scenario that solves the problem. L1 transcript; Awad notes

His own resolution of Bill or Jane

(His class version: an American firm's 5-year-old Saudi subsidiary needs a new marketing manager; Jane has 10 years' experience and an EMBA, Bill 8 years.) Nobody asked the two key questions: L1 transcript

Which city?Riyadh (more conservative)Bill
Jeddah (and, by his logic, Abha: less conservative than Riyadh)Jane

His closing line: "Neutrality is always required. Everywhere." L1 transcript

Rule 2: build a fact sheet before answering

His method for any case (his lecture 2 feedback on the homework case about Illy, an Italian espresso firm, facing Starbucks): L2 transcript

  1. Briefing: a short summary of each company.
  2. Fact sheet: a comparison table of the two companies on chosen factors.
  3. Then answer the questions, and draw suggestions, courses of action, advice and lessons for similar companies from the fact sheet.

Factors he suggested (an "endless list"; add or drop as needed): country of origin, nature of business, degree of diversification, type of customers (B2B or B2C), degree of international commitment, strategies (modes) of entry, competitors, competitive advantage (firm-specific advantages), strengths, weaknesses, opportunities, threats, potential. Lecture 4: the fact sheet for a country decision (the Poland / Gdansk case)

He came back to the fact sheet "again" for the Gdansk hand-in, this time as a weighted scoring table: list the factors, give each a weight out of 100 (its relative importance), score the country on each factor out of that weight (Poland gets 15 of the 20 for political stability), and add up the scores. L4 notes (Ahmed)

Factors to be consideredWeight (relative importance)Poland (actual score)Egypt
Political stability (sub-factors A, B, C, D)2015...
Economic environment (A: market size, B, ...)60......
... (other factors).........
Total100calculatedcalculated

"We can also add another market": one column for Poland and one for Egypt, and the highest total is chosen. Only the 20, 60, 15 and 100 are from the board; the Egypt column shows how to add a second market.

Explain it simply

It is a report card for countries. The weight says how much a factor matters to this company (here the economy counts three times as much as politics). The score says how much of that weight the country earns. The scores add up to one number per country out of 100, so the choice can be defended in a table and not just by feeling.

  • It is "more comprehensive than the bloody SWOT"; SWOT (and PESTLE) sit inside the fact sheet. SWOT is "just a suggested way" to organize information; there are many others. L2 transcript
  • Niche تسويق النيشات: a distinct special corner of the market "in a place on its own". A student said Illy is the niche (great espresso); he answered that Starbucks' sweets and gifts are niches too. L2 transcript

Lessons from the four lecture 1 cases

Lecture 1 came with four case pages: two full cases to hand in (Bill or Jane; Illy vs Starbucks) and two short "discussion examples" for class discussion only, numbered Example 2 and Example 4 on their page. Case folders

  • Illy vs Starbucks: country-specific advantages stay home; firm-specific advantages travel. A concept that wins in the US (paper cups, sweet milky drinks, to-go) meets a different "ecology" in Italy. Related diversification strengthens market position. Case 2-3 folder; L2 transcript
  • Bill or Jane: ask about the industry and the city; neutrality; culture shapes management decisions. L1 transcript
  • Example 2 (UK plastics maker copying US products under licence): success in the US failed in the UK because disposability was not yet accepted and the price limited it to the "AB" segment. Discussion examples folder My analysis: judging a foreign market through home eyes is the self-reference criterion; it is also an ethnocentric mindset. The "AB" segment = the richest buyers (social grades A and B). My analysis
  • Example 4 (sewing machine): a hobby in the US, a basic need in Nigeria, an heirloom and status symbol elsewhere. Same formal product, different core benefit, so the marketing mix must be differentiated. Discussion examples folder

Marketing ecology: the whole environment around a product in a market (culture and habits, income and prices, what people use it for, competition, infrastructure). Discussion examples page

12Coming later: topics he asks about but has not taught yet

Prof. Abu Qahf's past exams keep returning to a few topics that lectures 1-3 have not reached. Here is a short, plain picture of each, so the names already mean something when he teaches them. These are short previews only: the textbook pages are given for when the time comes.

Preview only Not yet taught. Read for orientation; study properly after he covers them.
The product life cycle (he drew it briefly on the board)

The ordinary product life cycle (marketing): a product's sales over time pass through introduction, growth, maturity, decline.

The international product life cycle (Raymond Vernon, mid-1960s): "a company will begin by exporting its product and later undertake foreign direct investment as the product moves through its life cycle", and "a country's export eventually becomes its import". Textbook pp. 168-169

  • Stage 1, new product: high-income home buyers; low volume, made at home near R&D; exports start late in the stage.
  • Stage 2, maturing product: demand rises at home and abroad; exports grow; the firm opens plants in the countries with the highest demand; some sales begin in developing countries.
  • Stage 3, standardized product: price competition; production moves to low-cost developing countries; the home country now imports the product; home production may stop.
  • Limits: built when the US dominated innovation; today new products appear everywhere, are launched in many markets at once, and many firms are international from birth.

Dunning's eclectic (OLI) theory: firms undertake FDI when Ownership advantages (a special asset such as a brand, technical knowledge or management ability), Location advantages (e.g. oil in the Middle East, a productive workforce) and Internalization advantages (doing the activity yourself rather than through an inefficient market) are all present. Textbook p. 206 His past papers ask to compare it with the international product life cycle.

Memory aid IPLC = "export first, invest later, import at the end". Dunning = O-L-I, all three needed.
Modes of entry into foreign markets (his favourite exam topic)

In lecture 1 he only split them into indirect (e.g. export) and direct (own plant, wholly owned or JV), and promised "more than four" indirect forms and an entry model of his own that he called the "Egyptian model" (not explained yet). L1 transcript The textbook's map: Textbook ch. 13, pp. 351-375

Global social responsibility: can MNCs be held accountable?

The booklet and a model-answer page from earlier batches give the same three answers: Booklet p. 8; past-exam page 6

  1. A global tax system: collect amounts from industrial and host countries and spend them on the pollution and poverty these companies cause.
  2. Accountability for environmental performance: measure environmental contributions (pollution and waste control); environmental assets and liabilities; reports and disclosure to society; a statement of financial position adjusted for environmental and social contribution.

Modern example The OECD/G20 global minimum corporate tax (15%, agreed in 2021) is a real-world step toward the "global tax system" idea, though it targets profit shifting, not pollution or poverty.

Abdelaal's 17 questions (tap to see the answer)

Q1. What are the requisite conditions for global standardization?
(1) The product must be capable of being globalized, and a global market segment must actually exist; (2) synergies from standardization; (3) infrastructure services (communications, transport, distribution channels). Explained here
Q2. What are the driving forces of globalization?
GATT (goods); GATS (services); drastic developments in communication and transport technology ("the death of distance"). Explained here
Q3. What are the constraints facing global standardization?
Internal: operational constraints inside the firm; lack of enthusiasm of local management. External: government trade restrictions; poor infrastructure or workers in the host country. Explained here
Q4. What are the 3 assumptions of the global standardization philosophy?
Customer needs are becoming homogeneous worldwide; people will sacrifice preferences in features, functions and design for a lower price at high quality; substantial economies of scale. Explained here
Q5. Globalization: scientific definition vs reality (the myth).
Definition: free mobility of everything (people, wealth, science, technology, problems) between countries without restrictions, a tendency to integrate the world. Reality: not a fact; visas, political disputes; burgers and jeans are only superficial symptoms. Explained here
Q6. The think / act matrix.
Think local, act local = domestic company. Think global, act local = global with minor alterations (e.g. the brand name in Arabic script). Think global, act global = standardized strategy. Explained here
Q7. The 3 objectives of the global management team.
Search worldwide for opportunities; maintain a presence in key markets; look for similarities among countries (e.g. Arab countries) to achieve economies of scale. Explained here
Q8. Modes of entry into foreign markets.
Indirect: exporting goods or services. Direct: FDI (own factory or subsidiary) or a joint venture. (Full entry modes come in a later lecture.) Explained here
Q9. The 3 levels of a product.
Core (the main benefit, the "why"); formal (features, size, colour, weight); augmented (services, warranty, guarantees, accessories). Explained here
Q10. Unity of command vs management by consensus.
Unity of command (USA/West): one subordinate, one boss, to avoid conflict; individualism. Consensus (Japan): many managers, 100% agreement before a decision; collectivism and Kaizen. Explained here
Q11. How are international organizations classified?
Multinational: a cluster of companies controlled by one headquarters. Multidomestic: each affiliate builds its own local strategy. Global: standardizes and integrates worldwide. Transnational: the UN's term, avoiding the colonial image. Explained here
Q12. Mission vs strategy.
Mission: what the company aims to be and why it exists. Strategy: the paths it selects to achieve its objectives. Explained here
Q13. Risk vs uncertainty.
Risk: predictable, and its financial consequences can be calculated. Uncertainty: cannot be predicted or calculated. Explained here
Q14. 4 major expressions of political risk.
Expropriation: seizure WITH compensation. Confiscation: WITHOUT compensation. Nationalization: the state takes a whole industry, without compensation. Profit blockage: profits cannot be transferred home. Explained here
Q15. The two strategic approaches to managing political risk.
Integrative: become part of the host society, build goodwill (local partners, suppliers, manufacturing). Defensive (protective): minimize exposure (small local footprint, key roles kept by the parent, local borrowing). Explained here
Q16. 5 red-flag indicators of organizational failure.
Turnover of skilled staff; under-investment in marketing; no new customers within 6 months; refusing new ideas; excess inventory with low turnover. Explained here
Q17. Key requirements of a TQM strategy.
His quiz lists 3: product diversification; employee empowerment; benchmarking. Write all 4: add the quality vision first (see the box above). Explained here

Model answer 1: globalization, its factors and indicators

Real questions: "Economic globalization depends on a number of factors: mention them without explaining; mention the conditional factors" (Paper A Q1). "Discuss in detail the phenomenon of globalization, explaining the driving and conditional factors, then the main features (two lines each) of globalization of supply, demand, strategy, competition" (Q3 on exam page 3, probably Paper A). "Mention briefly the indicators and the driving factors of globalization" (Paper E Q3). "Give the scientific term" for four signs of globalization (Paper K Q1, see Model answer 10).

Definition. Globalization is "the free mobility of everything between countries without any restrictions" (people, goods, services, capital, technology, even problems), or "the tendency toward integrating the world economically, politically and culturally". In practice it is a myth: visas, standards (the EU's CE mark), blocs and disputes restrict mobility; what we live in is "the death of distance".

Economic globalization depends on: IT and the Internet; companies' social and ethical responsibility; a global product or customer; global business standards; growth of trade, investment and their agreements; new competitors from emerging economies; fading borders.

Driving forces: the IT revolution; GATT (goods) and GATS (services) and trade liberalization; the end of the Cold War; progress in transport and communication; sudden global problems (pollution, AIDS, Covid-19); concentration of wealth and MNC dominance.

Conditional factors: the retreat of the state's power; the break-up of big countries (the Soviet Union); belief that globalization is inevitable; the belief that everything can be globalized; negation of national culture.

Indicators (types): demand: the same goods for different geographic segments (jeans, fast food, Pepsi); supply: a new international division of labour, component specialization, subcontracting; competition: from comparative to competitive advantage, strategic alliances; strategy: from economies of scale to economies of scope, moving activities between countries.

Conclusion. These are forces and symptoms; they push toward globalization, but "as long as there are restrictions, don't talk about globalization".

Two-word labels (Paper A Q1.2): strategic alliances = globalization of competition; fast food and jeans = globalization of demand; subcontracting = globalization of supply; scale to scope = globalization of strategy. Booklet p. 7

Model answer 2: is there a theory of globalization?

Real questions: "The justifications for the absence of a theory of globalization" (Paper B, 10 marks). "Is there a theory of globalization?" (Papers D and G). "The reasons for the absence of a theory of globalization" (Paper H, make-up for the first short quiz).

Answer: no. Globalization is a phenomenon, and "a phenomenon is not characterized by permanence"; a theory needs stable, general relationships. Moreover, even its definition is not met in reality: there is no free mobility of people, goods, technology or research (visas, EU standards, disputes), so it is a myth rather than a fact.

Justifications (booklet): (1) its governing principle is utilitarianism (النفعية: judging everything only by the benefit or profit it brings), leading to "market fundamentalism" (the market and profit rule everything) or "economic barbarism"; (2) it produces more prohibitions, impossibilities and dependency; (3) it leads to alienation and loss of freedom; (4) it conflicts with liberalism and with diversity, because it means extending influence and standardization; (5) the world's power "springs from diversity, not standardization"; (6) glocalization shows the contradiction: Ford, Coca-Cola and McDonald's standardize while Toyota lets the consumer decide what is produced.

Link to class. People mistake the driving forces (GATT, GATS, technology) and the superficial symptoms (burgers, jeans) for the phenomenon itself.

Model answer 3: indicators for predicting political risk

Real question: "Mention, using examples, some indicators for predicting political risk" (Q2 on exam page 3, probably Paper A). Also Paper H Q3 (without explanation) and Paper J Q2 (see Model answer 11).

Definition. Political risk is the likelihood that host-country political decisions or events will negatively affect a foreign firm's investment, disrupt its operations, or block its profit transfers. Because it is a risk (not uncertainty), it can be predicted and calculated, using indicators.

1. Economic indicators: high unemployment; declining living standards (which breed corruption and crime); high inflation; severe currency fluctuations.

2. Political indicators: frequent turnover of cabinets (six prime ministers or cabinets in Egypt 2011-2013); political kidnappings; extreme party fragmentation preventing consensus (Lebanon).

3. Cultural indicators: deep divisions of language, religion or region without a unifying national culture.

4. International indicators: hostility or conflict between the firm's home country and the host.

Other measures: Fortune and The Economist (bad neighbourhood, dictatorship, militarization, wars, extremist groups); intelligence units (internal and external variables); the political risk service (restrictions on ownership, transfers, tax discrimination); the handout's Table 7-1 checklist and Table 7-2 scoring.

Example. Egypt 2011-2013: political changes and violence meant no new foreign investors and many foreign and national investors withdrew.

Model answer 4: methods of managing political risk

Real question: "Discuss in detail the methods of managing political risk" (Paper B, 10 marks). Paper J Q2 asks the same "with at least two examples" (see Model answer 11).

Introduction. Managing political risk starts with a framework that identifies and rates the risks (Schmidt's three dimensions: political risks (transfer, operational, ownership-control), the general nature of the investment (conglomerate, vertical, horizontal), and its special nature (sector, technology, ownership; Type I to V)), or with quantification (scoring 30 criteria and adding them). Then the firm chooses responses.

1. Relative bargaining power. Keep the firm's bargaining power above the host's, e.g. through proprietary technology the host cannot replace; renew technology as it ages, because once the host's power overtakes the firm's, intervention occurs.

2. The integrative approach (become "less foreign", build goodwill): relations with local leaders and political groups; local manufacturing, national suppliers and local labour; subcontracting and joint ventures with local investors; local R&D; good labour relations.

3. The defensive / protective approach (minimize exposure): small local manufacturing footprint; locals kept out of key roles; borrowing from local banks (governments hesitate to nationalize firms indebted to their own banks); spreading production across several countries; R&D outside the host.

Choice. High-tech firms rely on defensive techniques; low-tech firms (steel) use both, mostly integrative; skilled-management firms (food) a balance; labour-intensive global-marketing firms (sewing machines) mostly defensive. In practice firms combine both.

Model answer 5: why global companies die (and how to keep competitive advantage)

Real question: "Mention without explanation: why do global companies die, or what are the indicators for predicting their death? How can global competitive advantage and control over the global market be maintained?" (Paper F Q2). The command word means a list is enough.

Indicators (Richard Watson, as the lecturer quoted him: a 2017 study of 500 US and 100 British firms, only 25 and 24 survive by 2027): (1) resignation of skilled staff; (2) under-investment in marketing; (3) no new customers in 6 months; (4) poor after-sales service; (5) no new products within 12 months; (6) rejecting new ideas (Kodak, Nokia); (7) excess inventory and marketing myopia; (8) no strategic planning and an aging board; (9) dependence on one supplier or customer (low external flexibility); (10) organizational hypocrisy and flattery; (11) inefficient information systems; (12) conflicts among owners and partners. Also: shrinking sales to loyal customers; falling reinvested profits; centralized decisions; promotion by seniority; excessive debt; high fixed costs; weak training budget; no diversification.

Keeping competitive advantage (his lecture 4 list, the one to write): continuous R&D (new and better or cheaper products, better production methods); a good database (quality, quantity, timing of information); add-on products; customer intimacy; continuous value added (customer retention: a new customer costs double); new techniques for the market; strategic alliances and joint ventures; global partnership with global firms; a global team; capitalizing on the waves of generations; simplicity; one selling appeal fulfilled rather than six half kept; investing in marketing; speed; diversifying the weapons against competitors; grasping competitors' success factors; continuous audit of everything; a smile. L4 notes (Ahmed)

Booklet version (p. 24): embrace the customer and respond fast; partner with suppliers and customers; understand the customer before competitors; accurate information; continuous R&D at low cost; complementary products; continuous added value; simplicity, commitment and speed; strategic alliances; keep promises; review environmental challenges; acquire competitors' success elements; global teams; ride generational waves; supportive structure; joint projects; invest in marketing with one clear promise.

Model answer 6: the new organizational models

Real question: "Mention briefly the most important features of the new models or forms of organizations in today's world" (Paper F Q3).

Feature: the 4 any's. The new model company competes any time, anywhere, any way, against anybody (Coca-Cola, Pepsi, P&G, Caterpillar, McDonald's).

Stage 1, TQM (necessary but not sufficient): quality vision ("company life and your job security depend on quality"); product diversification; employee empowerment (delegation, no micromanagement, accountability for results); benchmarking (Xerox).

Stage 2, the learning organization: transformation through learning and adaptation; requires creativity and innovation, openness, individuals' learning and self-confidence.

Stage 3, the World Class Organization: the elite of world companies (Sony, Honda); pillars: customer orientation, continuous cost and quality improvement, flexible organization and supply, creative HR, a just climate, IT support.

Why it matters: firms that fail to modernize these pillars die (Watson).

Model answer 7: DBA Q1, assumptions and requisite conditions of global standardization

Real question (DBA exam): "Point out: 1. three major assumptions relevant to the philosophy of global standardization; 2. the requisite conditions for global standardization."

Introduction. Levitt (1983) argued that technology drives the world toward one market, so firms should sell standardized global products and brands. Douglas and Wind (1987) showed this rests on three assumptions and works only under certain conditions.

Assumptions: (1) customer needs and interests are becoming increasingly homogeneous worldwide; (2) people everywhere are willing to sacrifice preferences in product features, functions and design for lower prices at high quality; (3) substantial economies of scale in production and marketing can be achieved by supplying global markets. Each has pitfalls: diversity within countries is growing (VALS), price positioning is vulnerable and buyers value quality (PIMS), and flexible automation plus the small share of production in total cost weaken the scale argument.

Requisite conditions: (a) the existence of a global market segment (big, loyal and reachable enough); (b) potential synergies from standardization (transfer of ideas, experience, expertise); (c) the availability of an international communication and distribution infrastructure. (Abdelaal's compiled class notes also add that the core product must be capable of being globalized.)

Conclusion. Standardization is one option on a continuum from pure standardization to pure differentiation; Exhibit 1: consider it only if there is a global segment, synergies, and no external or internal constraints.

Model answer 8: the Nike case (DBA Q2), using his fact-sheet method

Questions (question 2 of the DBA exam is a case about Nike in 1998): 1. What is the key to Nike's production strategy? Explain. 2. What are the advantages of frequent design changes in Nike's sneakers?

Brief. Nike, the US sports-shoe maker, sells more than 800 models for about 25 sports, held 33% of the world training-shoe market and 40% of the US in 1998, with sales over $9 billion. Its R&D centre in Beaverton (Oregon) designs the shoes; foreign contract factories make them. In 1998 it lost its "cool", stock piled up, profits fell, over 1,000 US workers were laid off, shoes were discounted in the UK grey market (Tesco), and reports on its Asian factories (e.g. Vietnam) damaged its reputation; Phil Knight apologized and the firm moved toward social responsibility and a back-to-quality Alpha line.

FactorNike (1998)So what?
Country of originUSA ("USA is a brand")Brand strength
Nature of businessDesign and marketing of sports shoes and wear; production contracted abroadKeeps the high-value activities at home
Degree of diversification800+ models, 25 sportsCovers many segments (niches)
CustomersB2C, global segment of athletes and youthA global market segment exists
Entry / operation modeContract manufacturing abroad (a non-equity contract); sales through a global brandLow capital, flexible, but less control
StrengthsQuality, R&D, "swoosh" brand, celebrity endorsementsPremium price, loyalty
WeaknessesUnsold stock 1998, image problemsWatson's red flag 7 (excess inventory), plus damage to its reputation (a social-responsibility threat)
ThreatsFashion shifts, grey markets, labour-practice criticismNeeds CSR and supplier control

Q1. The key to Nike's production strategy is "manufacture the highest quality product and the world is likely to beat a path to your door": high quality through continuous innovation (physiologists, engineers and stylists in Beaverton), while production is contracted to foreign factories. Nike keeps the core of its product (performance and design) and its brand at home and buys manufacturing abroad at low cost and with flexibility. The case also shows the limit: quality must include how products are made, so contracting abroad requires control of suppliers' working conditions (social responsibility).

Q2. Advantages of frequent design changes (each shoe updated at least every six months): (1) stays ahead of competitors and imitators; (2) gives customers a reason to buy again; (3) supports premium prices and the "cool" brand image; (4) uses the R&D centre's ideas quickly; (5) serves many segments (800 models, 25 sports); (6) makes copies and grey-market stock look old. Caution: fast changes raise the risk of unsold stock (1998), so production must follow demand closely.

Lesson. Quality, innovation and a global brand win markets, but without demand-driven production and social responsibility the same strategy creates a death signal (excess inventory, Watson's red flag 7) and a damaged reputation.

Model answer 9: DBA Q3, international commitment and the ethnocentric firm

Question: "Illustrate how to measure the international degree of commitment of a given multinational corporation, and point out without illustration the basic strategic orientation of an ethnocentric enterprise / MNE in terms of: a. basic company's mission; b. culture; c. human resource management."

Measuring the degree of international commitment (several measures together):

  1. Share of activity abroad: foreign sales, foreign employees or foreign investment as a share of the total; Rolfe: about 25% makes a firm international. Booklet p. 2
  2. Spread: the number of foreign markets served (one or more in his definition; six or more in Vernon's). L1 transcript
  3. Mode of involvement: from indirect (exporting) to contractual (licensing) to direct investment (joint venture, then wholly owned subsidiary): each step commits more resources and control. L1 transcript; Textbook ch. 13
  4. Management orientation: ethnocentric, polycentric, regiocentric, geocentric (Perlmutter): how far headquarters thinks and decides internationally. L1 transcript; Booklet p. 2
  5. Composite indexes: researchers (e.g. Sullivan, 1994) combine several such ratios into one index rather than relying on foreign sales alone. Online: Sullivan, JIBS 1994

The ethnocentric enterprise (home-country oriented, centralized):

Definition (Abdelaal's compiled lecture 2 notes): the mission is what the company aims to be and why it exists; the strategy is the paths it selects to achieve its objectives.

a. Mission: serve the home company's objectives; foreign units exist to sell the home product and return profits to headquarters.

b. Culture: the home country's culture and values are taken as the standard ("this works at home; therefore it must work in your country"); home standards are applied to evaluation and control.

c. HRM: home-country nationals are recruited, trained and placed in key executive positions at home and abroad.

Sources: Perlmutter (1969) as summarized in Wikipedia's "EPG model" article (home-country orientation, centralized decisions, home standards for evaluation, home-country recruits for key positions, checked online); booklet p. 2 (decisions at home head office; weakness: cannot adapt to the host). Chakravarthy and Perlmutter (1985) list the ethnocentric mission as "profitability (viability)"; I could not verify that table online, so treat this as unconfirmed.

Model answer 10: Paper K (terms, complete the sentence, draw only)

Why it matters: Paper K's topics (globalization, kinds of companies) were taught, and it uses three short formats that the other papers do not: give the term, complete the sentence, draw only. But several answers were not given in class: the 4 types of globalization (Q1), the conditional and governing factors (Q2.2-3) and the drawings (Q3) come only from the booklet's globalization chapter. Past exams; Booklet pp. 2-9

No.Term

2. From comparative to competitive advantageGlobalization of competition
3. Aggregating demand for the same good across many customer segmentsGlobalization of demand
4. From economies of scale to economies of scope; moving activities between countriesGlobalization of strategy

Memory aid from branch 4: D-S-C-S. The 4 indicators Booklet p. 7

Q2 (10 marks): complete.

1. "Companies can be classified into three main groups": (a) ethnocentric: centralized, all main decisions taken at head office in the home country; (b) polycentric: decentralized, the branches abroad set their own policies; (c) geocentric: integrated and spread worldwide, a large firm with material, human and technical resources (Perlmutter's patterns). L1 transcript; Booklet p. 2

Why this answer: in lecture 1 he used the same words for it: "Multinational corporations can be classified into three major groups ... the well-known classification ... ethnocentric ... polycentric; regiocentric; and even geocentric" (he said three, then listed four; the booklet gives the three above). See branch 2. If you have space, add one line: "Vernon and Livingstone also group them into GI (vertically integrated, high technology, extractive and manufacturing), GII (horizontally integrated, high technology, less politically sensitive) and GIII (transfer advanced technology to developing hosts through direct investment)" (booklet p. 3, not taught in class). Do not mix lists: multinational, multidomestic, global, transnational are names of firms, not these three groups.

2. Retreat of the state's power, belief that globalization is inevitable, negation of national culture = the conditional factors العوامل الشرطية. (The booklet's MCQs mark them as NOT driving forces.) Booklet pp. 7, 9, 11
