Model answer 11: political stability and FDI (indicators + managing, with examples)

Real question (Paper J Q2): "The degree of political stability in a country is one of the most important factors determining its attractiveness to foreign investment. Comment in detail, explaining: a. the indicators for predicting political risk; b. how a company can manage political risk in a given country (at least two examples)."

Comment. A foreign investor commits capital for years, so it fears political decisions or events that hit its ownership, its operations or its profit transfers. Instability raises this political risk, and because it is a risk (not uncertainty), it can be predicted with indicators and managed. Stable countries therefore attract FDI, and unstable ones lose it: in Egypt 2011-2013 no new foreign investors came and many foreign and national investors withdrew. L3 transcript

a. Indicators (E-P-C-I): economic (unemployment, falling living standards, inflation, currency swings); political (frequent change of cabinets, kidnappings, party fragmentation, as in Lebanon); cultural (deep divisions of language, religion or region); international (hostility between home and host country). Details: Model answer 3.

b. Managing it, two strategies with examples:

  • Integrative (become part of the host economy): a joint venture with local investors; buying from national suppliers and hiring local labour; local R&D; good relations with local leaders.
  • Defensive (reduce exposure): borrowing from local banks, because governments hesitate to nationalize firms indebted to their own banks; spreading production over several countries so no single plant is vital; keeping key technology and R&D outside the host.
  • Bargaining power: keep proprietary technology the host cannot replace, and renew it, so intervention stays too costly for the host.

Details and the firm types (Figure 7-4): Model answer 4, branch 7 D. Ch7; Elsere pp. 3-4

Conclusion. Political stability is not only a fact the investor finds; a good firm measures it with indicators before entering and manages it afterwards.

Model answer 12: comment on the definition of globalization, its theory, and accountability

Real question (Paper G Q1; Paper D Q1 is similar): "One researcher holds that globalization is the freedom of flow of people, capital, goods, services and the products of science between the countries of the world without restrictions, and that it is a trend toward integrating the world economically and politically. Comment in detail, then discuss: 1. Is there a theory of globalization? 2. Can international companies be held accountable for social responsibility?"

Comment. The statement joins his two definitions: the free mobility of everything without restrictions, and the tendency to integrate the world. As a definition it is correct, but reality does not meet it: people need visas, products must meet standards (the EU's CE mark), and blocs and political disputes stop flows. So globalization is a myth, not a fact; what exists is the "death of distance", pushed by driving forces (GATT, GATS, technology), and visible in superficial symptoms (burgers, jeans) that people mistake for the phenomenon itself. Branch 4 L1, L2 transcripts

1. Is there a theory? No. It is a phenomenon, and "a phenomenon is not characterized by permanence"; its governing principle is utilitarianism (النفعية: judging everything only by the benefit or profit it brings), leading to "market fundamentalism" (the market and profit rule everything); it leads to more prohibitions, impossibilities, dependency and alienation; it conflicts with liberalism and diversity; and glocalization shows the contradiction (Ford, Coca-Cola, McDonald's standardize; Toyota lets the consumer decide). Model answer 2 Booklet p. 8

2. Accountability for social responsibility. Assuming globalization is accepted in thought and practice, holding international companies accountable needs: (1) a global tax system that collects from industrial and host countries and spends the proceeds on the pollution and poverty these firms cause; (2) accountability for environmental performance: measure environmental contributions (pollution and waste control), give each area its assets and liabilities, publish reports, disclose to society, and adjust the statement of financial position for environmental and social contribution; (3) accountability for the "pollution of minds" is "a kind of the impossible", because globalization's mechanisms produce rebellion, escape and alienation. Booklet p. 8; past-exam PDF p. 6

Part 2 has not been taught in class yet; this answer is the booklet's. Also in Coming later.

Final mixed test (one from each branch)

1. "International business is the application of ... in different environments." Complete it.
... all managerial functions and theories and principles ...
2. What makes a firm international in his professional definition?
Doing business in one or more foreign markets, directly or indirectly; no cut-off point.
3. Why did the UN coin "transnational"?
To avoid the colonial image of "foreign" / "multinational" in former colonies.
4. Weakness of the polycentric pattern in 4 words?
Difficulty of control over branches.
5. Can the core be internationalized? What follows from yes and no?
Yes: go international (minor changes to formal/augmented levels). No: stay home.
6. "The market is not a place." Then what is it?
A group of people with needs to satisfy, desire to buy and purchasing power.
7. GATT and McDonald's: which is a driving force and which a symptom?
GATT = driving force; McDonald's = superficial symptom.
8. Name the 4 indicators of globalization.
Globalization of demand, supply, competition, strategy.
9. The three assumptions and three conditions of global standardization.
Homogeneous needs; sacrifice preferences for low price at high quality; economies of scale. Global segment; synergies; communication and distribution infrastructure.
9b. (Lecture 4) The 6 factors that govern the degree of standardization of the marketing program.
Type of product; heterogeneity / homogeneity of markets; media characteristics; government restrictions; infrastructure services; type of political relationship.
10. Task environment: list its 4 elements.
Customers, suppliers, competitors, government agencies.
11. Expropriation vs confiscation (class).
Expropriation with compensation; confiscation without.
12. E-P-C-I stands for?
Economic, Political, Cultural, International indicators of political risk.
13. Name two integrative and two defensive techniques.
Integrative: JV with locals; local R&D. Defensive: borrow from local banks; spread production over countries.
14. Which firm type relies most on defensive techniques (Figure 7-4)?
Labour-intensive, high value per weight, global-marketing firms (sewing machines); high-tech firms also rely heavily on defensive.
15. V-D-E-B?
TQM requirements: quality Vision, product Diversification, Empowerment, Benchmarking.
16. Managers vs engineers on quality spending?
Managers: saves ultimate cost, keeps customers (modern). Engineers: raises upfront cost (traditional).
17. Watson's numbers?
2017; 500 US + 100 British; by 2027 only 25 and 24 survive.
18. External flexibility ratio formula?
(Single supplier / total suppliers) x 100; higher ratio = less flexibility.
19. Three steps of his case method?
Brief each company; build a fact sheet (comparison table); then answer, suggest and draw lessons.
20. Dunning's three advantages?
Ownership, Location, Internalization.

14Glossary A to Z

Every key term in one place, for the last look on Wednesday morning. The definition is his or the handout's wording where one exists; click the term to jump to where it is explained.

TermArabicDefinition
Adaptive vs generative organizationAdaptive reacts to required changes but fails to anticipate them; generative (learning) anticipates change and has learned how to learn (handout Table 3-1).
AgentsالوكلاءIndividuals or organizations that represent one or more indirect exporters in a target market (paid by commission).
Augmented productالمنتج المدعمThe extra services around a product: guarantee, instalments, free cover.
Benchmarkingالبنشماركية / الأطر المرجعيةContinually measuring internal processes and products against industry leaders; "the standard or reference point against which things can be compared".
Case fact sheetHis comparison table of factors (origin, business, diversification, customers, commitment, entry modes, competitors, SWOT, potential), built before answering a case.
ConfiscationمصادرةTaking a foreign investment project with no compensation (class). Careful: the booklet uses the Arabic word مصادرة for taking with meagre compensation; answer in English.
Continuous improvement vs developmentالتحسين المستمرClass (lecture 4): improvement = small changes made all the time; development = huge changes. A learning organization = adaptation + continuous improvement.
Continuum (standardization-differentiation)"Continuum means scale": from pure standardization to pure differentiation, with hybrid strategies in between.
Convenience productسلع ميسرةA cheap everyday product bought often, quickly and with little thought (soft drinks, soap, razor blades); the easiest kind to standardize worldwide. One of the four classes: convenience, shopping, specialty, unsought.
Core productالمنتج الجوهريThe product "why": its function, the benefit the buyer enjoys.
Creativity vs innovationالإبداع والابتكارClass: creativity = something new with no previous example, the ideation component of innovation; innovation = the application of creativity, "not canned ideas" (Giza pyramid: new, no precedent, passes the time test).
Customer intimacyLecture 4, way 4 to sustain world class: manage the customer's expectations, let him participate, put yourself in his shoes, respond to his needs.
Customer retentionالاحتفاظ بالعملاءKeeping existing customers through continuous added value; "customer loyalty is an old school term", no customer is loyal. A new customer costs double an existing one (lecture 4).
Death of distanceموت المسافاتTransport and communication make distance feel smaller; geographic and cultural distance remain. What we live in, "rather than globalization".
Direct international businessالأعمال الدولية المباشرةOwn plant, subsidiary or branch abroad, wholly owned or a joint venture.
Driving forces of globalizationالقوى الدافعة للعولمةWhat pushes toward globalization (GATT, GATS, transport and communication technology); not globalization itself.
Eclectic (OLI) theoryDunning: firms undertake FDI when ownership, location and internalization advantages are all present.
Economies of scaleوفورات الحجمLower unit cost from larger volume; global firms reach it by exploiting similarities among countries.
EmpowermentالتمكينDelegating authority, no micromanagement, accountability based on results.
Empowerment (handout)التمكينThe process of giving employees the resources, information, and authority needed to carry out their jobs effectively (handout p. 76).
Ethnocentricالمركزي وحيد الجنسيةCentralized: all decisions and strategies made at headquarters. Weakness: cannot adapt to the host.
Expropriationنزع الملكيةClass: taking a foreign project with compensation. Handout: seizure "with little, if any, compensation".
External flexibility ratioنسبة المرونة الخارجية(Single supplier / total suppliers) x 100; a higher ratio means less flexibility.
Factors governing the degree of standardizationLecture 4: type of product; heterogeneity or homogeneity of markets; media characteristics; government restrictions; infrastructure services; type of political relationship.
Foreign direct investment (FDI)الاستثمار الأجنبي المباشرA lasting interest (10% or more ownership) in an enterprise in another economy; long-term, with the right to manage.
Formal productالمنتج الشكليThe features: size, colour, weight, design.
GATT / GATSGeneral Agreement on Tariffs and Trade (goods) / General Agreement on Trade in Services: driving forces of globalization.
Geocentricالجغرافي / العالمي التوجهLarge, integrated (vertically and/or horizontally). Weakness: imposes home-country culture.
Global companyالشركة العالميةA very large company that standardizes and integrates its operations, products, marketing and HR policies worldwide.
Global market segmentشريحة سوقية عالميةA group of buyers with similar needs in many countries; the first requisite condition for standardization.
Global productA product that can be marketed worldwide, satisfying customer needs on a worldwide basis.
Global sourcingالتوريد العالميThe use of worldwide suppliers, regardless of where they are located, who are best able to provide the needed output (handout Ch3 p. 83).
GlobalizationالعولمةThe free mobility of everything between countries without any restrictions; or the tendency toward integrating the world.
GlocalizationالعومحليةGiving things a local character within globalization (booklet).
Horizontal integrationالتكامل الأفقيThe same operation spread to different places.
Indigenization lawsLaws requiring nationals to hold a majority interest in the operation (handout).
Indirect international businessالأعمال الدولية غير المباشرةSelling abroad without one's own operation there, e.g. exporting.
Integrative techniquesالأساليب التكامليةMaking the operation part of the host's infrastructure, "less foreign": local relations, suppliers, JVs, local R&D.
International businessالأعمال الدولية(1) The application of all managerial functions, theories and principles in different environments. (2) Any organization doing business in one or more foreign markets, directly or indirectly.
International product life cycleدورة حياة المنتج الدوليVernon: a firm first exports, later invests abroad; the home country's export eventually becomes its import.
Joint venture (JV)المشروع المشتركA local and a foreign partner own the project together; the foreign side may contribute only know-how.
Learning organizationمنظمة التعلمAn organization able to adapt and improve continuously; needs creativity, openness, learning and self-confidence (class, lecture 4: adaptation + continuous improvement; creativity, openness, self-efficacy). Handout: "able to transform itself by anticipating change and discovering new ways of creating products and services; it has learned how to learn"; openness, creativity, personal efficacy (p. 78).
LicensingالتراخيصA licensor grants a licensee the right to use its intangible property for a specified period.
Macro political riskالخطر السياسي الكليRisk that affects all foreign and national firms across the economy.
Management by consensusالإدارة بالإجماعNo decision without 100% yes from everyone; success and failure are everyone's responsibility.
MarketالسوقA group of people with needs to satisfy, desire to buy and purchasing power. "Not a place."
Market fundamentalismأصولية السوقThe belief that the market and profit should rule everything (booklet p. 8: where utilitarianism leads globalization).
Marketing ecologyThe whole environment around a product in a market (culture, income, use, competition, infrastructure).
Marketing myopiaShort-sightedness: looking at your own product instead of at what customers want (red flag 7 of company death).
Mass customizationTailor-making a standard product to each customer's expectations (Dell) so it is not seen as a generic offering (handout p. 70).
Micro political riskالخطر السياسي الجزئيRisk targeted at particular foreign firms or industries.
Multidomestic companyالشركة متعددة المحليةAffiliates in many countries, each with its own strategies, based on perceived differences between countries.
Multinational corporationالشركة متعددة الجنسياتA cluster of companies spread in different countries and held by the headquarters.
NationalizationالتأميمTurning private (foreign) ownership into state ownership; no compensation (class).
NegotiationالتفاوضBargaining with one or more parties to arrive at a solution acceptable to all.
Nicheالنيش (ركن سوقي متخصص)A distinct, special corner of a market. (Niche marketing = تسويق النيشات.)
Objective vs targetObjective = long-term result (business continuity); target / aim / goal = short-term result (immediate profit).
Pattern standardizationالتوحيد النمطيOne global theme or positioning, executed locally.
Personal efficacyThe belief that one both can and should learn to influence significantly the world in which one lives; built by self-awareness and proactive problem-solving (handout p. 80).
Political riskالخطر السياسيThe likelihood that host-country political decisions or events will negatively affect a foreign firm's investment, disrupt its operations, or block its profit transfers.
Political systemالنظام السياسيThe structure, processes and activities by which the nation governs itself.
PolycentricاللامركزيDecentralized: each subsidiary sets its own policies and strategies. Weakness: hard to control.
ProductالمنتجAnything, tangible or intangible, that has characteristics that satisfy a human need.
Product proliferationCreating a wide array of product versions that competitors cannot copy quickly enough (Canon); one of three approaches to innovation (handout p. 71).
Protective and defensive techniquesالأساليب الدفاعية والوقائيةDiscouraging host interference by staying non-integrated: small local plant, R&D outside, local borrowing, spread production.
Push vs pull (retail)Push: manufacturers push goods onto stores and customers. Pull: the retailer identifies needs and customers pull goods from the store (Wal-Mart) (handout p. 82).
RegiocentricOrganized and decided by region.
Relative bargaining powerقوة المركز التفاوضيKeeping the firm's bargaining power above the host's, e.g. through proprietary technology.
RiskالخطرAn event that can be predicted and whose occurrence can be calculated.
Self-efficacyالكفاءة الذاتيةClass name (lecture 4) for the third requirement of the learning organization, tied to empowerment; = the handout's personal efficacy, the booklet's self-confidence.
Self-reference criterionJudging a foreign market through your own culture's eyes.
Six sigmaMotorola's quality target: under 3.4 defects per million parts (3 sigma = 66,810; higher sigma, fewer defects) (handout pp. 68, 77).
Target costing (Japan)Planned selling price minus desired profit = target cost; every component is costed with designers, engineers and suppliers, then cost is cut continuously (handout Figure 3-6).
Task environmentبيئة المهامThe external competitive or specific environment: customers, suppliers, competitors, government agencies.
Technology paradoxHigh-tech MNCs can thrive while their prices fall fastest: cut prices, win share, profit from the follow-on market (handout pp. 69-70).
Total business environmentبيئة الأعمال الكليةInternal environment plus external (public / general and task / specific) environment.
Total Quality Management (TQM)إدارة الجودة الشاملةPillar 1 of the new model firm; requires quality vision, diversification, empowerment, benchmarking.
Transnational corporationالشركة عابرة القوميات / عبر الوطنيةClass: the UN's term for an international firm, chosen to avoid the colonial image of "multinational" or "foreign". Booklet: a firm combining global integration with local responsiveness.
Uncertaintyعدم التأكدAn event that cannot be predicted, so its occurrence cannot be calculated.
Unity of commandوحدة الأمرEach subordinate takes orders from one manager only, to avoid contradictory orders.
UtilitarianismالنفعيةJudging every action only by the benefit it brings ("the greatest good for the greatest number": Bentham and Mill). Booklet p. 8: the governing principle of globalization, so there is no theory of it.
Vertical integrationالتكامل الرأسيUpward toward the market, downward toward raw materials.
Virtual organizationالمنظمة الافتراضيةDoes business as if it were a very large enterprise while it is much smaller: core competencies kept, the rest outsourced (handout p. 83).
Weighted fact sheet (country scoring)Lecture 4, for the Gdansk case: factors weighted out of 100 (political stability 20, economic environment 60, ...), each country scored, highest total chosen.
World Class Organization (WCO)طبقة الصفوة من الشركاتThe elite of world companies, able to compete anywhere, any time, any way, against anybody. Handout: "enterprises that are able to compete with anybody, anywhere, anytime, anyway"; 6 pillars (p. 81).
